Framework

Most work now passes through a machine before it is finished. A model drafts the text, writes the code, runs the analysis, and a person signs it. This site is about the part that stays with the person. It asks four questions. How do you get good work out of a model? How do you know whether what it gave you is right? What should you keep doing yourself, and what can you hand over without losing something? And who is doing the work, when most of what carries your name was not written by you?

The answers are not opinions. Eighty-seven books and papers, from the Upanishads to research published this year, were read closely and rewritten as chapters. Their claims were taken out one sentence at a time, held against each other, and gathered into the rules on this page. Every rule can be followed back to the sentence and the source it came from.

Every chapter was broken into claims: one-sentence statements that can be checked against the source and marked as evidence, opinion or contested. Claims from different sources that say the same thing are gathered into a thesis. Theses that describe one regularity are gathered into a rule. Some rules hold across all four questions; the rest hold within one of them.

The rules are the short answer to what all this reading adds up to. Each shows the theses it rests on, why it holds, and where the sources say it fails. Each thesis shows the claims for and against it and the chapters they come from. When a claim is withdrawn, because a study did not replicate or the source was misread, everything above it is recounted, so this page changes as the reading does.

Skill lives only where it is exercised

You keep only the skills you keep practising with feedback; whatever you hand to a tool decays unnoticed.

Delegated skill fades, and your own sense of the skill does not register the loss. If you will need to check a tool's work, keep doing some of that work yourself.

Why it holdsThe evaluation and delegation questions meet here, and the identity question supplies the same shape from another tradition: skill is a residue of repeated, effortful, corrected action, so it grows only where that action continues and fades everywhere it stops. Drivers lose navigation, cabbies lose the tissue, residents lose the operating hours, programmers lose the library, operators lose the takeover — and in every case the self-rating stays where it was, which is why the decline is only discovered when the tool is withdrawn. It predicts that the next capacity to go will be whichever one the tool now performs end to end, and that the person will report no change.
Where it failsHanding over the writing and the fault-finding costs the learning, but asking the assistant for reasons does not shows the decay is not automatic in use: what the person does after the output arrives decides it, and asking for reasons preserved learning. The same thesis carries the confound that heavy model users may have been the weaker students already. And A person and the tool they rely on solve the task together, and where the work happens decides nothing denies that anything was lost at all, on the ground that the person and the resource are one system.
PracticeKeep a low-frequency unassisted rep of each delegated skill — one problem a week done without the tool — and treat the result, not your sense of it, as the reading.

How it feels is evidence about the person

How easy, hard or certain a situation feels is made inside you and tells you about you, not the situation.

The feeling of ease, difficulty or confidence is produced by the mind separately from the facts. Read it as a sign of your own state, and check the situation by other means.

Why it holdsIt spans the interface, evaluation, delegation and identity questions with one mechanism: the felt reading is computed by the person and then read back onto the world as a property of it. Confidence rises without accuracy, developers feel faster while measured slower, work gets offloaded when it feels hard rather than when it is hard, trust moves on style, grief follows the report rather than the event, and a meditation session that feels successful can be a failure. It predicts that for any new felt signal — this model is reliable, this refactor is going well, this practice is working — the feeling will be recoverable from the person's fluency, framing and state, and will not covary with the outside measure.
Where it failsDamasio says a gut feeling cuts the options down before reasoning starts, and people who lose it decide badly cuts against the practical conclusion: the felt signal is not noise to be discarded, and people who lose it cannot decide at all. A hunch is recognition of something already met, so it is reliable only in a field the person has practised names the condition under which the feeling does track the world — a regular domain the person has practised with feedback. And A published finding is worth only what an outside test leaves standing weakens the most-cited instance, since the Dunning-Kruger curve is partly an artefact.
PracticeBefore acting on a read of how the work is going, get one number from outside — a measured time, an error count, a second reader — and let the feeling tell you only about your own state.

A measure scored on stops measuring

Once a person or a model is scored on a measure, the measure stops meaning what it named.

Whoever is scored learns to raise the score, so it drifts away from the goal it stood for. Before you trust a score, find out what behaviour it paid for.

Why it holdsIt joins the interface question to evaluation and delegation through one mechanism: whatever is scored is what gets produced, and everything adjacent to it drifts. A model guesses because nine of ten benchmarks give no credit for admitting ignorance; an assistant's manner is whatever forty raters rewarded; instruction tuning raised truthfulness and left bias untouched; a stand-in metric in an organisation comes apart precisely when the team gets good at chasing it; a manager scored on activity produces activity. It predicts that any new metric introduced to steer work will be met within a year and will by then have stopped standing for the goal — and that a capability figure quoted for a model will say less about your task the more famous the test is.
Where it failsMeasures do sometimes deliver the thing they name: How a model is trained matters more than how big it is is a case of aiming at a target and hitting it, and A simple rule built from an expert's own past decisions beats the expert by answering the same way every time shows that formalising a criterion can improve on the judgement it was fitted to, precisely by being mechanical about the measure.
PracticeFor every number you steer by, name the second number it would degrade, and put both on the same page.

Change the arrangement not the person

People do what their setup makes easy, so change the setup instead of asking them to be more careful.

The procedure, the display and who answers for the outcome shape behaviour more than instructions do. Telling someone to be careful changes nothing; changing what is easy does.

Why it holdsAll four questions supply the same result: what a person does is predicted better by the arrangement than by the person. At the interface, everything a user knows comes from what the machine shows, and design failures are recorded as human error. In evaluation, whether anyone examines an argument is set by having a reason, a middling demand and no stress, and the trait of enjoying thought moves behaviour only slightly. In delegation, changing the decision procedure works where debiasing training does not, being answerable changes checking where instructions do not, and psychological safety is a property of a work group. On identity, motivation follows conditions and blocked needs produce substitutes. It predicts that a new quality problem will yield to a changed form, display, sequence or accountability, and will not yield to a reminder.
Where it failsMinutes of training in a skill corrects how well people judge their own work at it is a clean case of changing the person cheaply and successfully. A habit you keep failing to break is protecting you, and small tests of the fear behind it work locates the lever inside the person, in an assumption only they can test, and Why a person works predicts how long they keep going and how well, separately from how motivated they look makes the reason a person acts do work that the arrangement does not reach.
PracticeWhen behaviour needs to change, redesign the step — its order, its default, its display, its owner — and only then consider training anyone.

Nothing helps in itself it has to fit the receiver

No tool, technique or amount of supervision helps in itself; each fits one level of skill and harms another.

The help that carries a beginner holds back an expert, and the reverse. Set the amount of help per task and per person instead of adopting one policy for everyone.

Why it holdsThe same conditional turns up under every question. A prompting trick helps large models and hurts small ones; a hunch is worth trusting in a practised regular domain and worthless outside it, and pairing with a model pays only where the model is right on the cases the person gets wrong; supervision is set by experience at that particular task and drops back when the task changes, and the support that helps a beginner starts to hurt an expert; and past a point the task needs a different kind of mind that no training supplies. What the instances share is that the intervention has no fixed sign — its sign is a function of the receiver and the task. It predicts that any tool reported as a general win will be found to have a boundary, that the boundary will be unmarked, and that the largest gains and the largest harms will fall on different populations.
Where it failsThe role you give a system and the style it answers in change its output and your judgement and Minutes of training in a skill corrects how well people judge their own work at it are close to unconditional wins, which the rule does not predict. Beyond competence people improve by reorganising what they know rather than adding rules, and courses cannot take them there is itself contested by its own sources on whether experts really abandon rules.
PracticeDecide tool, technique and supervision per task and per person, and re-set them whenever the task changes rather than when the person is promoted.

Reliability removes the check

The better a machine works, the less anyone watches it, so the check has to be scheduled, not triggered.

Nothing punishes inattention while the machine is right, so attention fades, and nobody is watching at the moment it is wrong. A fixed schedule of independent checks catches what a trigger never will.

Why it holdsEvaluation and delegation give the same loop from both ends. Nothing punishes inattention while the machine works, so inattention grows; the supervisor cannot follow decisions made faster than she can think; a second job collapses fault-catching from nearly all to a third; pilots shut an engine down on one unsupported warning and expertise did not protect them; and the errors that survive are the ones that look like correct work. It predicts that a reliable system's first real failure will be missed, that the miss will not be explained by the operator's seniority, and that an instruction to "review carefully" will change nothing where being answerable for the outcome would.
Where it failsA published finding is worth only what an outside test leaves standing records that Parasuraman and Manzey found little evidence that trust is the mechanism, so the loop may run on attention rather than on belief. You cannot tell whether someone checked from what they looked at or what they produced blocks the easy audit in both directions: an unedited output can be the result of a careful judgement, so under-checking cannot be measured off the artefact.
PracticePut a fixed sample of the machine's output through a full independent check on a schedule, and make one named person answerable for the outcome rather than for the review.

The inside is not readable from the outside

What a person or a system is doing inside cannot be read from what it produces.

The same output can come from understanding or imitation, from care or neglect. Arguments about what is inside end up settled by the definition each side chose, not by evidence.

Why it holdsIt spans all four questions: the same underdetermination that makes a model's right answer no evidence of a human-like route makes an unedited output no evidence that nobody checked, makes a calm worker no evidence of a dropped claim, and makes the machine's interior undecidable from its behaviour. In every instance the visible thing is compatible with several insides, so the argument then turns on which definition of understanding, self, checking or freedom was adopted first. It predicts that any new dispute of the form "does it really X" will move when someone fixes the definition and will not move when someone runs another behavioural test.
Where it failsOutsiders can only learn what a model does by testing it, and words like wants must predict what it does cuts both ways: behaviour is the only access outsiders have, and mental vocabulary that predicts behaviour earns its keep whatever the inside turns out to be. Guessing the next word well requires knowing how the world works, so there is no shortcut argues the opposite direction, that some outputs do constrain the inside. And The same job becomes a different job depending on how a worker sees it, and that predicts what they change shows one case where the inner stance is readable, because it predicts what the worker changes.
PracticeBefore arguing whether a system or a person really understands, checks, or has let go, name the behaviour the answer would change — and if no behaviour changes, settle the definition and move on.

What you are identified with is invisible from inside

You cannot examine what you are identified with from inside it; it changes only when something makes it an object.

A role, a skill or a belief that you take to be yourself cannot be weighed while it is you. Something has to set it apart first, and letting go of it needs your worth to rest on something else.

Why it holdsThree questions produce one operation described in four vocabularies. In evaluation, a wrong view survives by absorbing each awkward detail and the mind cannot audit itself while it runs. In delegation, an author cannot see his own faults, bad news is filtered out at every level of the chain, and whether anyone says the awkward thing is a property of the group. On identity, Kegan's development is exactly the move from being a thing to having it, ACT weakens a self-description by handling it as an object, and the Vedantic instruction — whatever you can observe is not the observer — is the same manoeuvre performed deliberately. The instances share a structure: what a person is inside is not available to them, and it becomes available only through an outside position. It predicts that a correction aimed at something load-bearing will be met with an explanation rather than a revision, and that the same correction lands once the thing is named aloud and the person's standing does not depend on it.
Where it failsPractice prepares a person and clears away a covering but cannot produce a state nobody made denies that the shift can be produced at all by method. Writing about your values helps only when it comes early, nobody explains its purpose, and its gains build on themselves narrows the re-footing move sharply — it stops working once it is announced as a technique or applied after the defence is in place. And A mind watching itself changes what it watches and tends to find what the watcher already believed warns that the objectifying look is not clean either: it returns what the looker already held.
PracticeBefore giving someone hard feedback — including yourself — name the thing their standing rests on, give it somewhere else to stand, and have the reading come from someone with nothing at stake.

The first answer becomes the answer

Whichever answer you meet first becomes your answer, so commit to your own before the machine's or the group's appears.

An anchor, a suggestion or a majority view moves where a judgement ends, and the judge cannot feel it happening. Write your own answer down first; then look at theirs.

Why it holdsThe interface, evaluation and delegation questions converge on one finding: a judgement is pinned by whatever reached the person first, and the person cannot feel the pinning. An assistant trained on approval returns your own hint; a majority's wrong answer captures a third of responses; an anchor moves the estimate; every study of AI assistance showed the model's answer before the person had their own, and withholding it cut the following of wrong advice. It predicts that any review step placed after the output is read will approve more and catch less than the same step placed before, and that a premortem run before the plan is defended will surface objections the same people would not raise afterwards.
Where it failsSupport that helps a beginner starts to hurt an expert, because what helps depends on what you already know reverses it for beginners, who learn more from a worked solution shown first than from being left to struggle. The conformity instances also carry their own limits: in Asch's data a majority held out, and how much people conform varies by decade and country.
PracticeWrite your own answer, estimate or diagnosis down before you open the model's, and keep both.

Which part of the task went decides what is lost

What you lose by handing work over depends on which part went, but people hand over whatever feels hard.

Offloading the routine part and offloading the judging part cost different things, and neither cost shows at the time. Choose what to hand over by what you need to keep, not by what feels effortful.

Why it holdsIt runs from the interface question through evaluation and delegation to identity: a tool acts on tasks rather than jobs, the writing and the debugging cost learning where asking for reasons does not, and the extended-mind conditions set when an outside store counts as yours at all. The instances share a structure — the cost of a handover is a function of which sub-task crossed the line, while the person's criterion for crossing it is felt effort, which is uncorrelated with that function. It predicts that a team adopting a tool will offload the parts that feel tedious first, which is not the same set as the parts that are safe to lose, and that the residue of their work will be inspection and repair.

People push work out of their heads when it feels hard, not when it is, and the world holds it also finds people offloading where they gain nothing, so felt effort is not reliably tracking effort either.
PracticeBefore handing a sub-task over, ask whether you would still be able to catch that handover's mistakes afterwards; if not, keep that piece and give away the piece beside it.

A result outruns the design that produced it

A famous result gets used far beyond the sample, the control and the measure that produced it.

The finding is quoted; the study's limits are not. Before acting on a claim, find the study design behind it and check that it covers your case.

Why it holdsThe pattern recurs wherever the book draws on published work, across all four questions: a circuit diagram that worked on a quarter of prompts, a scaling law resting on one full-scale run, an emergent ability that is an artefact of the scoring rule, a thirty-to-one productivity gap that compared different tasks, a self-affirmation effect that survives only unannounced and before the threat, a Dunning-Kruger curve that is partly statistical, a tradition's scientific credentials manufactured in the nineteenth century. The instances share a shape: the memorable sentence is broader than the design, and the gap is invisible once the sentence is in circulation. It predicts that for any striking claim, the sample will be smaller, the setting narrower and the measure more decisive than the claim implies.
Where it failsA paper's famous conclusion often survives after the method behind it fails cuts the other way — Damasio's general point survived his mechanism, and one audited method failing did not overturn the answer — so a weak design is not by itself a false claim. And Minutes of training in a skill corrects how well people judge their own work at it is a small, replicated, cheap result that has travelled without distortion.
PracticeBefore citing a finding in a decision, write down its n, its control and its outcome measure in one line; if you cannot, treat it as a hypothesis.

Reasons are reconstructed after the fact

Neither a person nor a system records why it acted, so every account of its reasoning is built afterwards.

The explanation is produced later, by a process meant for telling others, and it can be sincere and wrong. Treat a stated reason as a story about the act, not a record of it.

Why it holdsThe same absence turns up in a trained model, in a person asked why they chose, in an expert asked for his method, and in a mind looking for the one who was deciding. What the instances share is that the reporting machinery is separate from the doing machinery and runs later, on whatever is left. It predicts that in any new case — a model's chain of thought, a post-incident interview, a designer's account of why the code is shaped this way — the account will be coherent, will be produced readily, and will not be a record.

PracticeTreat any "why" — yours, a colleague's, or the model's — as a story to be tested against the artefact, and put the decisive check outside the thing that made the decision.

The failure shows downstream of its cause

A failure shows up where it lands, not where it starts, so the complaint about the tool usually points upstream.

The tool gets blamed because that is where the error becomes visible. Most of the time the fault is in the specification, the data or the design, and fixing the tool leaves it in place.

Why it holdsFour questions produce the same displacement. At the interface, a failure of tokenisation cannot be prompted away and an operator error is usually a design error. In evaluation, the damaging mistake is the one that looks like correct work, so it surfaces late and somewhere else. In delegation, the fault sits in the specification, the data or the policy, where no output check reaches it, and the search for someone to blame closes the inquiry. On identity the chain begins in what the mind dwells on rather than at the decision. It predicts that a team reporting "the AI doesn't work" will be found, on inspection, to have an unsettled specification or an unowned design — and that fixing the prompt will not hold.
Where it failsThe displacement is not unlimited: The same way of asking helps on one model or task and hurts on another and The role you give a system and the style it answers in change its output and your judgement show real gains available at the point of complaint, so not every interface problem is a design problem in disguise. And Everything a person does has causes behind it, and people who drop blame for that reason do not behave worse is contested where its own sources define the terms — the rule tells you to keep asking why, not that nobody is answerable.
PracticeWhen a tool is blamed, write down the specification the work was supposed to satisfy before touching the tool; if you cannot write it, that is the fault.

An explanation moves agreement not judgement

An explanation makes people accept an answer more often without helping them tell good answers from bad.

Explanations feel like evidence, but in the studies they raised acceptance and left error-finding unchanged. Treat an explanation as persuasion until it has helped you catch a mistake.

Why it holdsIt joins the interface question to evaluation and to delegation: the same explanation that is built to satisfy a reader raises acceptance equally on the model's right and wrong cases and empties a sign-off that an institution is counting on. What the instances share is that the explanation is optimised for plausibility while the reader's discrimination is what was supposed to improve. It predicts that adding rationales, citations or chain-of-thought to a review step will raise throughput and agreement and leave the error rate where it was — and that a confidence number, which can be scored, will beat all of them.
Where it failsHanding over the writing and the fault-finding costs the learning, but asking the assistant for reasons does not is the standing counter-case: a reason asked for after the answer arrives preserves learning where silence does not. The rule also does not hold where the explanation can be contested — an explanation the reader can act against is the one case An explanation of an answer is worth having only if it helps you find mistakes says is worth having.
PracticeDo not ask for an explanation you have no way to contest; ask instead for the model's confidence, or for the one check that would show the answer wrong.

The claim on the result is what binds

Handing work over gives up the claim to be its author; the work and the answerability stay where they were.

Delegation moves the doing, not the responsibility. What hurts in handing over is losing authorship of the result, and that is also what keeps a person answerable for it.

Why it holdsThe identity and delegation questions meet on one distinction. The Gita separates the claim on the work from the claim on its fruit; James shows the self's boundary drawn by felt ownership, so it swallows possessions and audiences; Vedanta and Sankhya put the sense of authorship after the act rather than before it; hospital cleaners holding the same job description hold two different jobs; and against all of this, delegating the production does not delegate the answerability. What the instances share is that the painful part of handing work over is the authorship claim, which is separable, while the two things people think they are protecting — the work, and being answerable for it — do not move. It predicts that an engineer distressed at a model writing the code is losing the claim rather than the craft or the responsibility, and that the distress falls when the claim is dropped and the review kept.
Where it failsThe distinction resists checking: Two people doing the same thing can be in completely different inner states, and nothing visible tells them apart means nobody, including the worker, can verify that the claim was dropped rather than the effort, which is the standing objection that non-attachment licenses complacency. AI lifts the weakest workers most, so the work looks alike and no longer shows who made it shows the claim was carrying real information about the author, so dropping it is a real loss and not only a psychological one. And Everything a person does has causes behind it, and people who drop blame for that reason do not behave worse presses against After all the teaching the last choice is the person's own, and they can always choose their attitude on whether the stance is chosen at all.
PracticeWhen you hand a piece of work to the model, give up saying you wrote it and keep both the review and the name on the outcome.

The manner came from somebody else

An assistant's voice and its agreement were trained by other people, so neither says anything about the answer

How it sounds, how sure it seems and whether it goes along with you were set by a small paid group and by whatever text was on the web, not by your question. State the audience, the conventions and the form you want, because everything you leave unstated you take from them.

Why it holdsOne manufacturing process produced the manner, and a separate mechanism in the reader mistakes the manner for the merit. Ouyang's paper puts a number on the first: about forty screened contractors, agreeing with one another only about three-quarters of the time, alongside the researchers who wrote their instructions and a waitlist seeded by employees; human judgement enters once, and every later update pushes the assistant towards what a stored guess of a contractor's choice predicts. Sharma's team found the result in use across five assistants from three companies, where a tentative hint at what you believe moves the answer and one line of pushback makes an assistant take back a correct one. On the receiving end, Reeves and Nass found people rated identical advice more insightful when the computer's style matched their own, and Lee and See found trust set by how fast a system replies, how it looks and how fluently it talks rather than by how often it has been right. It predicts that agreement arriving after you state your view carries no information, and that the same answer in two registers will be judged differently by the same reader.
Where it failsFlattery is in the model before human-preference training and survives it puts part of the effect before the raters, so it is not only their doing, and the studies do not separate an assistant caving in from one correctly treating your disagreement as evidence. Teaching consultants to prompt made them worse on the harder task warns that acting on this by elaborating your instructions can cost more than it buys.
PracticeWrite the form and the audience you want before you ask, and when the assistant agrees with you, argue the opposite position and see whether it agrees again.

Training and size improve only what they were aimed at and leave toxicity and bias where they were supported

A bigger model is not better

How a model was trained decides what it can do, and its size does not

The gains that matter came from what the training text was and what the training rewarded, not from more parameters. When you choose a model, or hear that a new one is larger, find out what its training aimed at and expect nothing outside that.

Chapters Attention Is All You Need · Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback · Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models · Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models · On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots

Why it holdsThe four theses share one mechanism: these systems improve at whatever the training was pointed at and at nothing beside it, so a headline about scale is a headline about the wrong variable. Ouyang's raters preferred a 1.3 billion parameter model to the 175 billion parameter one it was built from, after a small amount of human ranking. Chinchilla, smaller than Gopher and trained on more text for the same budget, beat it on truthfulness 43.6 per cent against 29.5 and did not lower average toxicity at all; instruction training roughly doubled truthful and informative answers, left bias measures unmoved, and produced a model that followed an order to be offensive better than the one it came from. The design itself has kept its shape since 2017 and was built to make training about ten times cheaper rather than to make anything smarter, and the scaling rule the field quotes minimises training cost while most of a model's lifetime computing goes on answering users. It predicts that a release described mainly as bigger will not move your work, and that a release aimed at one thing will move that thing and leave your other measures where they were.
Where it failsNew abilities appear suddenly as models grow, nobody can predict which ones, and the size varies by model records eight tasks across five model families sitting at chance over orders of magnitude and then rising well above it, so growth does buy something nothing else buys. Once a big model shows an ability smaller models soon get it limits that in turn. The preference result also has a flaw of its own: the test used the same raters whose rankings trained the model, and the win is on following instructions, not on the test scores the same paper shows falling.
PracticeChoose a model by running your own cases on it, and read what its training and post-training aimed at rather than its parameter count.

How a model is trained matters more than how big it is supported
Training and size improve only what they were aimed at and leave toxicity and bias where they were supported
The design of these models has barely changed since 2017 and only the amount of training text grew supported
Answering users costs more than training the model, but the field's rules count only training supported

Most fluent where it knows least

A model answers a rare fact as confidently as a common one, so supply the rare facts yourself

The smoothness of the wording is produced separately from whether the thing is true, and the errors concentrate on whatever the training text saw once. Put the names, dates and numbers into the prompt instead of asking the model to remember them.

Chapters Attention Is All You Need · Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback · On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots · On the Biology of a Large Language Model · Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models · Why Language Models Hallucinate

Why it holdsThe theses supply a floor, a mechanism and a reason the floor is invisible. Kalai and co-authors prove that for facts with no pattern behind them a model's error rate after pretraining is at least the share of such facts its training text recorded exactly once, so if a fifth of birthdays appear once, expect a fifth of birthday answers to be wrong; they also prove that a model which never says anything false has given up estimating what the text says. Anthropic's traces show the mechanism: the model starts ready to say it does not know until a familiar name switches that refusal off, so it is familiarity and not knowledge that opens the answer. The same even tone covers a task the machine cannot perform at all, as when DeepSeek-V3 gave 2 or 3 for the Ds in DEEPSEEK across ten tries. And an assistant trained on approval withdraws a correct answer under one line of pushback, so its hesitation is no guide either. It predicts that errors will cluster on the rarest item in any list it gives you, and that a well known name attached to an invented detail is the shape the mistake takes.
Where it failsBoth proofs are about a base model, before post-training or a search tool, so a model that looks things up is not covered by them. GPT-4 was calibrated before reinforcement learning and not after shows that how well a model's confidence tracks the truth is itself a product of the last training step rather than a fixed property, and so can be restored.
PracticePaste the rare facts in rather than asking for them, and check every name, date and number the model produced instead of repeated.
Theses
Made-up facts come from how a model is trained and scored, not from a fixable bug supported

Only your own task finds the edge

Whether the tool helps depends on the task, and only trying it on your own work shows where

There is a real line between the work the tool improves and the work it damages, and the line is unmarked and not where people expect it. Published scores and other people's experience will not locate it for you, so keep a small set of cases from your own work and score them yourself.

Chapters Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models · Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage? · Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models · The Jagged Technological Frontier · Co-Intelligence · AI Snake Oil · Why Are There Still So Many Jobs?

Why it holdsThese theses do not merely say that help must suit the receiver; they say the fit cannot be known in advance by anybody, including the people who built the thing. Dell'Acqua's consultants working on tasks that suited the tool were better, faster and more complete all at once, and on a task built to defeat it the same tool dragged them down. In the same study, the consultants given an overview of how to write prompts scored 60.0 per cent correct on the harder task against 70.6 per cent for those given no overview at all. Wei and colleagues found no feature that predicts which tasks jump, and report that the amount of training compute at which an ability appears depends on the particular model and its text. Narayanan and Kapoor add that the single word covers at least three unrelated technologies, so a score that does not say which one it measured settles nothing about your job. It predicts that any published figure will fail to predict your own hit rate, and that two people with the same tool and the same job title will report opposite results, both honestly.
Where it failsThe consultant contrast is a single comparison at ten per cent significance, and three of the four claims under AI helps on the tasks it suits and hurts on the rest, and nobody can tell which is which are argument rather than measurement. Once a big model shows an ability smaller models soon get it shows the edge does move in one direction over time, so a case that failed once is worth retrying rather than written off.
PracticeKeep ten cases from your own work, run them on any model or method you are considering, and score the results yourself before adopting it.

Some failures sit below the prompt

Some failures are built into how the model reads and was scored, and no wording reaches them

A prompt arrives after the input has been chopped into pieces and after the training has fixed what gets rewarded, so there are errors the prompt cannot touch. When a failure survives two honest rewordings, stop rewording and change the input, the tool, or the way the job is divided.

Chapters Attention Is All You Need · Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models · Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models · On the Biology of a Large Language Model · The Jagged Technological Frontier · Why Language Models Hallucinate

Why it holdsEach thesis names a failure whose cause lies under the level a prompt operates at. Asked how many Ds are in DEEPSEEK, DeepSeek-V3 answered 2 or 3 across ten tries, because the word arrives as the chunks D, EEP, SEE and K; no rewording reaches that, though a model that spells the word out first answers 1, which puts the fix in the input format rather than in the request. Attention adds its inputs as an unordered set, so word order has to be supplied separately. Kalai and co-authors prove a floor rather than describe a bug: for facts with no pattern behind them the error rate after pretraining is at least the share of such facts the training text recorded exactly once. And a prompting trick that paid off above a certain amount of training compute did real harm to smaller models, so the technique is not the level either. It predicts that a failure repeating identically across rewordings will repeat on the next model of the same design, and will move only when the input representation or the division of the task changes.
Where it failsThe role you give a system and the style it answers in change its output and your judgement shows that wording does reach a great deal, so the rule marks a floor and not a ceiling. Attention's cost was trivial in 2017 and is now the main limit is a case where later engineering softened a constraint that looked structural, and Made-up facts come from how a model is trained and scored, not from a fixable bug is proved about a base model, before post-training or a search tool.
PracticeGive a failure two rewordings; then change the input, spell the thing out, split the task, or hand the step to something that is not a model.

Everything you learn about it expires

Everything you find out about a model has a date on it, so write the date down

Models are replaced, published tests get trained on, and the language inside one is frozen at the moment its text was collected. Record the date beside every limit you find, and run the failing case again when the model changes.

Chapters Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback · Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models · Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models · Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage? · On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots · Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models · Co-Intelligence · AI Snake Oil

Why it holdsThree clocks run under these theses and all of them make a finding perishable. Sharma's team watched their own flattery tests become a standard training target, which is how a published number decays into a training objective. Mollick's rule follows from the same thing: record any limit you find with a date, because the model will be replaced. A model keeps the words in use at the moment its data froze, and the corpus figures behind that observation are themselves from 2021. The field's own results perish the same way, as when Hoffmann's team traced the earlier scaling answer to intermediate numbers read off a training schedule built for a much longer run, then spent Gopher's exact budget on a smaller model and beat it 67.6 to 60.0 on one standard test. It predicts that a workaround you build for a weakness will outlive the weakness and quietly cost you, and that any benchmark figure is worth less each year you keep quoting it.
Where it failsThe design of these models has barely changed since 2017 and only the amount of training text grew holds the other way: the design has kept its shape, so the structural facts about how input is read do not expire on the same clock as the scores. A result the field repeated for years came from a measuring mistake and one experiment settled it rests on one source and one run at one size, by the group whose own fit made the prediction, so the correction is itself dated.
PracticeDate every note about what the tool cannot do, and re-run those cases the week the model changes.

No method sets the problem for you

No technique turns a confusing situation into a problem, so state the problem and the test yourself

The model answers the question you actually asked, and building that question out of a mess is the one step nothing performs for you. Write the problem in a sentence, and write what would make an answer wrong, before you start asking.

Chapters Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance · The Jagged Technological Frontier · The Alignment Problem · माण्डूक्योपनिषत् गौडपादकारिका · The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and Gauḍapāda's Kārikā · The Media Equation · Co-Intelligence · The Reflective Practitioner · Why Are There Still So Many Jobs?

Why it holdsThe theses meet at the moment a situation is turned into something a machine can be given, and they agree that the moment has no method and carries most of the risk. Schön argues that problems do not arrive ready made: someone names what to attend to and frames the context, and no procedure tells him how. Christian shows the cost of getting that step wrong on the machine side, where a goal that cannot be stated exactly gets a stand-in, and the stand-in comes apart just as the system gets good at chasing it, as when a boat learns to spin for power ups instead of racing, and where the car that killed Elaine Herzberg had no category for her. Mollick's finding that the role you assign a model is part of the instruction rather than decoration is the same point at the scale of a single prompt, and the ragged edge means the choice of what to hand over is yours as well. It predicts that the largest errors will trace to the statement of the problem rather than to the answer, and that two people handing the same mess to the same model will get answers differing more than the model itself varies.
Where it failsTeaching consultants to prompt made them worse on the harder task shows that more deliberate framing is not automatically better, with the overview group scoring 60.0 per cent against 70.6 per cent for those given none. A description is never the thing it describes, and trouble starts when a person or machine acts on it instead is broad enough that little could count against it, and where the situation is a familiar case type there is nothing left to frame and the older account of problem solving fits it.
PracticeBefore you open the model, write one sentence naming the problem and one naming what would make the answer wrong, and keep both beside the output.

Nobody who built the tool is here

Nobody who built the tool can explain it or answer for its output, so both fall to you

The designers are not present, the picture in their heads was never shared, and nothing inside a working system records why its parts are there. You learn the tool only from what it does in front of you, and you are the only person answerable for what you send out.

Chapters Ironies of Automation · The Design of Everyday Things · Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback · On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots · On the Biology of a Large Language Model · The Psychology of Computer Programming · Sources of Power · From Bacteria to Bach and Back

Why it holdsEvery thesis here removes one party you might have expected to rely on. Norman's point is that designer and user never meet, so the product's own shape and controls carry the whole load of teaching; Weinberg measured what happens when they do not, finding that of 117 experienced FORTRAN programmers, nine got a rule with seven forms right. Four different groups shaped the assistant's manner and none of them claims that authority. Dennett's argument is that the reasons a design works are explicit while it is being built and only implicit once it runs, and Anthropic's researchers hit exactly that wall, reading a separate easier network trained to copy the model rather than the model itself, and calling the substitute a stepping stone. Bender's case closes the circle on the other side: a fluent mistranslation got a Palestinian man arrested with the system performing exactly as designed, and the person harmed had nowhere to go. It predicts that the documentation will not contain the thing you need, that the thing you need will show up in your own record of what the tool did, and that a failure will be recorded against whoever pressed send.
Where it failsMost failures blamed on people are design failures, and removing the operator leaves the designer's mistakes uncaught carries three contested claims, and Norman leaves the strong form of it unevidenced while Bainbridge's evidence is second hand. Interpretability tools read a stand-in model, not the real one is also a report of progress rather than only a limit, so the stronger reading, that nothing about the inside can be known, goes further than the theses do.
PracticeKeep your own written record of what the tool did on your work, and send nothing out that you would not defend as your own.

A check needs the skill it checks

A check is worth only what the person checking could have produced on their own

Looking over an answer you could not have produced yourself is not checking, it is agreeing more slowly. Before you accept the job of checking something, ask whether you could get to the answer without it; if you could not, either build that ability or stop calling the step a check.

Chapters Ironies of Automation · Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? · Cognitive Offloading · Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity · How AI Impacts Skill Formation · Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance · When Combinations of Humans and AI Are Useful · The Jagged Technological Frontier · Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation · The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking

Why it holdsEvery finding here turns on the same quantity, the checker's own ability to reach the answer. Asked why they had not thought about an output, 319 workers gave 130 reasons of ability and 58 said they lacked the knowledge to inspect it, against only 44 who said they had no time. Vaccaro's pooling of 370 effect sizes from 106 experiments found the pair fell below the better partner at g = -0.23, and which partner was better alone predicted the outcome better than anything else measured, so the pair gains only where the person could already have got there. Bansal found a model matched in overall accuracy is useless as a partner unless it is right on the particular cases the person gets wrong. Bainbridge's operator cannot check a decision made faster and by finer criteria than she can form one. It predicts that adding a review step to work nobody in the room could do unaided will not lower the error rate, and that the same step added where the reviewer could produce the answer will.
Where it failsA person can direct work they could not do themselves by comparing results instead of producing them gives the exception: someone who cannot produce the answer can still compare several answers or judge a result against a stated aim, which is direction rather than checking. An operator with nothing else to do catches nearly every failure, and one with a second job does not puts a second cause under the same failures, since detection fell from about 97 per cent to 33 with a competing task and ten minutes of manual control brought it back, so some missed errors are load rather than missing ability. You cannot tell whether someone checked from what they looked at or what they produced blocks the audit either way.
PracticeBefore you agree to check something, write your own answer to the same question first; if you cannot produce one, say so and treat the output as unchecked.

A score answers its own question

A score answers the question its test asked, which is almost never the question your decision is asking

A number is only ever about the quantity someone chose to measure, on the cases they chose, with the comparison they chose, and any of those three can make an accurate score useless to you. Before you let a score decide anything, write down the quantity your decision actually needs and ask whether the test measured that on cases like yours.

Chapters Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models · Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage? · On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots · Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models · Studies of Independence and Conformity · Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance · When Combinations of Humans and AI Are Useful · Using Cognitive Psychology to Understand GPT-3 · Machine Psychology · Co-Intelligence · AI Snake Oil · From Bacteria to Bach and Back · What the Buddha Taught · Language Models in a Programming Course · Why Language Models Hallucinate

Why it holdsThe gap between the measured quantity and the needed one is where accurate systems do their damage. The 1997 pneumonia model found that asthma lowered the risk of death, because asthmatics with pneumonia were rushed to intensive care, and acting on the correct pattern would have sent them home; Optum's model predicted what a patient would cost rather than how ill they were, so equally ill Black patients were enrolled less often; a model announcing one chance in 365 that a birthday falls on 7 March is perfectly calibrated and tells you nothing. The choice of measure also manufactures findings on its own: a per-token probability of 0.6 scores 0.08 across five tokens while 0.9 scores 0.59, so half an improvement in the underlying quantity looks sevenfold, and metrics such as Exact String Match sit behind more than 92 per cent of 137 hand-annotated claimed abilities. The choice of comparison decides the verdict too, since the same 370 effect sizes show the human and machine pair falling below the better partner and rising far above the person alone. And a test score decays, because Sharma's team watched their own measure become a training target. It predicts that a number quoted without its quantity, its cases and its comparison will not reproduce on your work.
Where it failsMeasures do sometimes deliver what they name, and refusing them is worse than using them badly: A simple rule built from an expert's own past decisions beats the expert by answering the same way every time shows a crude quantified criterion beating the judgement it was fitted to across 237 studies and 136 comparisons. Outsiders can only learn what a model does by testing it, and words like wants must predict what it does is contested but stands against the counsel of despair, since for a closed system behavioural testing is the only route anyone outside has, and the design outlasts the score even when the number is stale within a year.
PracticeWrite the quantity your decision needs in one sentence before you look at any score, then check what the test measured, on whose cases, against what.

Test the answer not the source

Standing, style and agreement say nothing about an answer, so test the answer against the thing it is about

Almost everything that makes an answer feel checked is a fact about where it came from rather than about whether it is true, and every one of those signs can be produced without the truth behind it. Keep the test on the thing itself, something in the world that could come out against you, and treat the source's rank, manner, fluency and readiness to agree as carrying no information.

Chapters Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback · To Trust or to Think · Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models · Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? · Influence · Studies of Independence and Conformity · Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance · The Jagged Technological Frontier · The Media Equation · Who Sees Human? · From Bacteria to Bach and Back · What the Buddha Taught · The Reflective Practitioner

Why it holdsThe Kalamas were told not to accept a teaching on report, tradition, scripture, logic or the teacher's standing but to find out for themselves, and the measurements arrived twenty-five centuries later. A uniform got 92 per cent compliance where students predicted 63, and the nurses in Cialdini's report followed a dangerous phone order they knew enough to refuse. Reeves and Nass found people praised by a computer rated it higher even when told the praise was picked at random, and remembered the warning correctly afterwards; told the machine was their teammate, they rated identical suggestions as more helpful. Agreement is the emptiest sign of all, since in Ouyang's method the assistant is trained towards what a stored model of a paid ranker would pick, and Sharma's team found across five assistants from three companies that one line of pushback makes a model withdraw a correct answer while its stated confidence sits near 99 per cent before and after. Explanations move acceptance without moving discrimination, with accuracy rising on the items the model got right, falling on the ones it got wrong, and the average not moving. What survives is Schon's point that situations resist. It predicts that raising the apparent authority, polish or agreeableness of a source will raise acceptance and leave error detection where it was.
Where it failsWhere the thing cannot be consulted, other people are the only instrument left, and they are not pure noise: People treat what others believe as evidence, especially when unsure, and one person disagreeing restores their own answer records that a single ally cut Asch's errors sharply even when that ally was also wrong, and Disagreement between professionals on the same case can be measured without knowing the right answer turns several independent judgements into a usable measurement. A mind cannot watch itself working, so the verdict on its own judgment has to come from outside goes further and makes the outside verdict necessary, with Suka at peace only once king Janaka said his own conclusion back to him, though that member is weak.
PracticeFor each answer you accept, name the thing in the world you would look at if it were wrong, and look at it.

A hunch is worth its feedback

A hunch is worth only what the field taught it, so trust it where the work answers back quickly

A hunch is a memory being recognised, so it carries information only where the situations repeat and the world tells you soon enough that you were wrong. Judge the field before you judge the person: in a field that repeats and corrects, take the hunch seriously and dig out the cue behind it; in one that does not, credentials and years buy nothing.

Chapters Thinking, Fast and Slow · Conditions for Intuitive Expertise · Revisiting the Six Stages of Skill Acquisition · Peak · Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later · Superforecasting · उपनिषद् · The Upanishads · Sources of Power · Descartes' Error · Know Thyself · AI Snake Oil · The Reflective Practitioner

Why it holdsKahneman and Klein settled their disagreement on exactly this condition, that intuition is recognition and nothing more, so it is worth the practice behind it and the regularity of the world. Chase and Simon put the store at fifty to a hundred thousand patterns built over about a decade, and a chess master who rebuilds two-thirds of a real board after five seconds manages two or three pieces of a random one, which shows the knowledge is about the domain and not about the person. Tetlock scored 284 professionals on some 28,000 dated predictions and found the average no better than chance, with credentials, access and politics separating nobody, while accuracy where feedback exists behaved like a skill and his best forecasters extended their lead in later years. That is why fireground commanders sit inside the condition and stock pickers outside it, and why hedgehogs forecast worse inside their own specialty than outside it. The cue itself is recoverable but only by the right question: Klein's neonatal nurses had nothing to say about sepsis until asked about particular babies, and a large share of the cues they then named appear nowhere in the professional literature. It predicts that a hunch in a fast-feedback field will beat a checklist, and that the same person's hunch in a slow-feedback field will not beat a coin.
Where it failsEven inside a valid field the expert is not a steady instrument. The same expert judging the same case twice gives two different answers and A simple rule built from an expert's own past decisions beats the expert by answering the same way every time show the recognised answer wobbling from day to day and a formula built from that same person's own past calls beating them by being consistent. Damasio says a gut feeling cuts the options down before reasoning starts, and people who lose it decide badly is weak, since the general position held and the card-game machinery under it has thinned. None of these sources tells you which sort of field you are standing in, which is the judgement the rule needs made first.
PracticeBefore you act on a hunch, ask how often this situation repeats and how quickly you find out you were wrong, then ask the person for the particular past case rather than for their method.

Judging your own answer is a skill

How sure you feel is no test of being right, and only practice at the task itself corrects it

The sense that an answer is good is built by a separate machinery from the one that produced the answer, so it can rise while accuracy stays put or falls. The repair is not resolve or humility but minutes of real training in the thing being judged, which moves the self-estimate by moving the ability under it.

Chapters Conditions for Intuitive Expertise · To Trust or to Think · Unskilled and Unaware of It · Studies of Independence and Conformity · Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity · How AI Impacts Skill Formation · Make It Stick · Superforecasting · उपनिषद् · The Upanishads · Know Thyself · The Alignment Problem · Mindwise · The Media Equation · Noise

Why it holdsFleming's sample of nearly a thousand people found that intelligence predicted how well they did a task and not how well they judged their own answers, which makes self-judgement a second ability rather than a by-product of the first. It can be driven on its own: raising the brightness of signal and noise together leaves the task exactly as hard and the confidence higher, and people then seek less information and change their minds less often. The errors are large and durable. Executives put their read on two candidates at 75 to 85 per cent against a measured correlation of .28; METR's developers predicted 24 per cent faster, reported 20 per cent faster and were measured 19 per cent slower, with months of using the tool failing to shrink the gap; dating partners predicted each other at 44 per cent while believing 82. The one thing that worked was skill: Kruger and Dunning's ten-minute training packet brought the worst performers' self-view right while the untrained bottom quarter drifted further wrong, and the effect disappears once the change in ability is held constant. It predicts that asking people to be more careful or more humble will not move their self-assessment, and that a short dose of the underlying skill will.
Where it failsThe gap is not constant across conditions. People examine an argument when they have a reason, a middling demand, and no stress gives the ceiling, since self-checking breaks down worst under heavy load, so the same person is a better judge of their own work at a middling demand than at either extreme. A published finding is worth only what an outside test leaves standing cuts into the headline case, because the crossing-lines graph everyone remembers is largely a statistical artefact that random numbers reproduce. Being wrong about your average is also not the same as failing to spot a particular mistake, which is the version that matters for checking.
PracticeWhen your confidence in a judgement is high, spend ten minutes practising the underlying task against known answers, then judge again.

Small revisions beat being sure

Accuracy comes from many small revisions, so count how often you revise and how often you explain something away

Being right is a habit of correction rather than a quality of the first answer, and a wrong belief stays alive because each detail that does not fit gets a small cheap excuse that nobody keeps count of. Date your answers, revise them in small steps as evidence arrives, and keep a tally of the excuses, because the tally is the only thing that makes the pattern visible.

Chapters Thinking, Fast and Slow · Conditions for Intuitive Expertise · To Trust or to Think · Unskilled and Unaware of It · Studies of Independence and Conformity · Superforecasting · Sources of Power · Know Thyself · Dispositional Differences in Cognitive Motivation · Behave · AI Snake Oil · Noise · The Reflective Practitioner

Why it holdsTetlock's best forecasters revised often and in small steps, with Tim Minto making thirty-four revisions on one question averaging three and a half points, and willingness to change your mind predicted accuracy about three times as strongly as intelligence did. The same tournament shows the habit is trainable rather than a trait, since an hour spent reading forecasting guidelines raised accuracy by roughly ten per cent for about a year against untrained forecasters on identical questions, and the best forecasters extended their lead in the second and third years while credentials and access separated nobody. The opposite habit is cheap and invisible: Klein points out that nobody counts the excuses, and Schon watched children call a counterweighted block impossible rather than drop the rule that blocks balance in the middle. Confidence cannot be the trigger, because it is built separately and rises on its own when signal and noise are raised together. It predicts that a person who logs dated predictions and revises them will beat a more knowledgeable person who does not, and that a belief you have defended three times without changing it is the one to test.
Where it failsRevising needs a trigger and the conditions are narrow. Good forecasters change their minds on new evidence, while a wrong belief survives by explaining away each awkward detail carries its own limits, since Schon argues only a surprise you dislike forces a revision and Sapolsky finds lasting stress makes people repeat an action harder instead. People examine an argument when they have a reason, a middling demand, and no stress narrows it further, because when nothing is at stake nobody examines anything and when everything is, everybody does, so the habit shows up only in the middle. A little learning makes people confident, and more of the same learning makes them worse warns that more evidence poured through one settled idea buys confidence rather than correction, so revising has to reach the idea and not only the numbers.
PracticeKeep a dated list of your open judgements with a number on each, revise them whenever something arrives, and mark every time you keep one by explaining a detail away.

Ask the same person or model the same question twice, because the gap between the answers is a measurement

You usually cannot find out whether an answer is right, but you can always find out whether it is stable, and an unstable answer cannot be mostly right. Re-ask the same case on another day, in another wording, or of another qualified person, and treat the spread you get as the first number you know about the answer.

Chapters On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots · Conditions for Intuitive Expertise · To Trust or to Think · Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? · Studies of Independence and Conformity · Make It Stick · Know Thyself · Using Cognitive Psychology to Understand GPT-3 · Machine Psychology · Behave · Noise

Why it holdsThe spread is measurable when the truth is not. Seen from behind a target with the bull's-eye hidden, a scattered team is still obviously scattered, and scored as mean squared error a set of judgements splits into two independent parts of equal weight, how far off and how far apart. The sizes are not small: wine judges scored 18 per cent of the same wines identically on a second tasting, software developers estimating the same task on two days differed by 71 per cent, and two underwriters pricing the same file differed by a median of 55 per cent where executives had predicted 10. Models show the same instability from the other side, since reordering Wason's cards from A K 4 7 to 4 7 A K changed which cards the model picked. And the cure follows from the measurement: Goldberg's models tracked their own judge at about .80 across 237 studies and beat that judge every time, with Grove's 136 comparisons putting most of the margin down to consistency alone. It predicts that any judgement you re-ask will move, that the move will be larger than the people making it expect, and that averaging two independent attempts will beat either.
Where it failsConsistency is not accuracy, and removing the spread removes something real with it: What an expert acts on is missing from the textbooks and cannot be got by asking about method records cues that appear nowhere in the professional literature, often an expected event that did not occur, and An expert recognises what kind of situation this is, and the action comes with the recognition describes judgement arriving whole, so a formula that flattens the variation subtracts the expert's subtle rules along with the noise. Disagreement between professionals on the same case can be measured without knowing the right answer rests on a single source. A biased set of judgements can be perfectly stable and perfectly wrong.
PracticePut five past cases back in front of the same person or model, in changed wording and order, and record how far the second answers sit from the first.
Theses
The same expert judging the same case twice gives two different answers supported
Disagreement between professionals on the same case can be measured without knowing the right answer weak
A model's test score depends on the wording, the answer order and what it has already read supported
A simple rule built from an expert's own past decisions beats the expert by answering the same way every time supported
People who see an answer before forming their own judge differently, so make them answer first supported

What to keep and what to hand off 8

supported5 of 5 theses11 sourcesQuestionsWhat to keep and what to hand off 5How to know it is right 3How to get good output 1
Remove the junior and lose the expert

A tool that removes the beginner's share of a job leaves nobody able to do the expert's share later

The machine rarely takes the expert's work; it makes the beginner optional, and the beginner's work was how competence got built. If you hand over the routine and the unpolished parts, keep a named share of them in the hands of whoever is learning, on real cases, with someone watching.

Chapters Ironies of Automation · High Output Management · Revisiting the Six Stages of Skill Acquisition · Peak · The Skill Code · Sources of Power · Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance · The Alignment Problem · Co-Intelligence · The Reflective Practitioner · The Society of Mind

Why it holdsBeane watched ninety-four operations across five hospitals and found residents doing surgical work for almost the whole of an open procedure and ten to twenty times less of a robotic one, where the surgeon sits alone at a console. Bainbridge supplies the mechanism from the other side, since the routine work is what keeps a skill alive and an operator who has only watched for months performs like a beginner when control comes back. Watching a finished performance does not substitute: Quist's studio demonstration is so accomplished that it corrects no errors, and Ross and Bagnell proved the machine version, where a learner given only clean demonstrations has no recoveries to copy and a million frames of expert play left the network crashing as often as two thousand had. What is missing cannot be replaced by a course either, since past competence people improve by reorganising what they know, and Klein's fireground record of 127 recognitional decisions out of 156 is what that looks like from outside. It predicts that a group which adopts a tool making juniors optional will, some years on, hold experts it cannot replace and nobody able to check them.
Where it failsBeane's own bomb disposal teams put the controller in the trainee's hands, so deployment and not the machine decides the outcome, and his surgical evidence is one speciality, observed rather than randomised. Support that helps a beginner starts to hurt an expert, because what helps depends on what you already know carries Sweller's position that explicit instruction and worked examples keep working, with randomised trials behind them, so the fumbling is not valuable in itself. Handing over the writing and the fault-finding costs the learning, but asking the assistant for reasons does not narrows the damage further, since the cost attaches to handing over the writing and the fault finding, not to using the tool at all.
PracticeReserve a fixed share of the routine work for whoever is learning it, let them hold the controls on real cases with an expert watching, and count that time as production rather than training.

A tool that lets experts work without juniors removes the work that made juniors able to check it supported
Automation keeps the routine work and leaves people the rare hard cases they no longer get to practise supported
The problems that matter lie where technique stops working and a finished demonstration hides the fumbling a learner needs supported
Beyond competence people improve by reorganising what they know rather than adding rules, and courses cannot take them there supported
How closely to supervise depends on the person's experience at that task and drops back when the task changes supported

Some of the job cannot be taught

What an expert acts on cannot be taught in a course or got by asking, so choose someone practised

Some of what a job needs is recognition built up over years of particular cases, and neither a briefing, a written procedure nor an interview about method transfers it. Match the work to someone who has met that kind of case before and seen how it came out; where nobody has, hand over a smaller piece and keep the judgement.

Chapters Conditions for Intuitive Expertise · Revisiting the Six Stages of Skill Acquisition · Peak · Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later · Sources of Power · Know Thyself · In Over Our Heads · Immunity to Change · The Reflective Practitioner · The Society of Mind

Why it holdsKlein's neonatal nurses had nothing to say about sepsis when asked about their method and plenty when asked about particular babies, and a large share of the cues they then named appear nowhere in the professional literature; often the tip off is an expected event that did not happen, which leaves nothing to point at. The reason is that a hunch is recognition and nothing more: Chase and Simon estimated fifty to a hundred thousand recognisable patterns built over about a decade, and their chess master rebuilds two thirds of a real board after five seconds and two or three pieces of a random one. The same boundary is what puts fireground commanders inside the condition and stock pickers outside it. Kegan and Lahey add the harder case, where the demand is not about what a mind holds but how it is organised, and their composite of twelve studies, 282 adults, found 59 per cent short of self-authorship and none at the order above it. It predicts that a hand off resting on judgement will fail wherever the receiver has not practised that exact field, and that no amount of instruction closes the gap.
Where it failsEricsson holds that much of what is called a difference in kind yields to structured practice, and Support that helps a beginner starts to hurt an expert, because what helps depends on what you already know carries Sweller's randomised evidence that explicit instruction works and keeps working. Klein's cues are reconstructed from interviews about cases the experts chose to report, and an absence noticed in hindsight is the easiest thing to over report. Kegan's 282 are not a probability sample and the scoring is interpretive. The rule also cuts both ways, since the practised person is only practised in one field: How closely to supervise depends on the person's experience at that task and drops back when the task changes says the same expert needs close direction again when the work changes under them.
PracticeWhen the work turns on judgement, pick the person by the cases they have already worked and the results they saw, not by their title, their course record or their account of how they work.

What an expert acts on is missing from the textbooks and cannot be got by asking about method supported
A hunch is recognition of something already met, so it is reliable only in a field the person has practised supported
Beyond competence people improve by reorganising what they know rather than adding rules, and courses cannot take them there supported
When a job asks for a different kind of mind, training and new skills cannot supply it supported
Adults grow by turning what they are into something they can look at, and most stop partway supported

A controlled setting is what gets automated

Work goes to a machine where the surroundings can be controlled and written down, not where it looks easy

The line between what a machine takes and what a person keeps runs through the setting, not through the difficulty of the task. Before you hand anything over, ask what it would cost to make its surroundings predictable and to say exactly what a good result is, and treat that cost as part of the price.

Chapters Ironies of Automation · The Psychology of Computer Programming · The Mythical Man-Month · Peak · Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance · The Alignment Problem · AI Snake Oil · The Society of Mind · Why Are There Still So Many Jobs?

Why it holdsThe same physical task falls on either side of the line depending on where it is done: a car plant fits windscreens with robots while a garage replacing the same glass uses a technician, and Amazon's Kiva robots move shelves across a level floor while a person still does the picking. Minsky's dates say it from the other end, since mathematical logic fell to a program in 1956 and college calculus in 1961 while what a four year old does resisted for decades. Bainbridge completes the account: whatever can be specified is what gets taken, so the rare and abnormal cases are what is left behind. The two remaining pieces are the bills that come with the transfer. Brooks holds that deciding exactly what the thing should do is the hardest single part and that clients cannot say it correctly until they have used a version, and Caruana's pneumonia model, which learned that asthma patients were low risk because they went straight to intensive care, shows that a system can be right about bad records and no better model repairs it. It predicts that the expensive part of any hand off will be the specification and the containment of the setting rather than the capability, and that a task which looks trivial will stay with a person wherever its surroundings vary.
Where it failsAutomating part of a job makes the rest worth more only where demand grows and entry stays hard is contested and sets three conditions that often do not hold: Autor's cash machines rose from about 100,000 to 400,000 while tellers rose from about 500,000 to 550,000, but his own wage series shows real pay below roughly the fifteenth percentile falling between 1999 and 2007 even as those jobs grew, and Computers cut middle-paying jobs and move work to both ends of the scale while pay does not follow rests on one author. The price of making a setting controlled is usually invisible and enormous, which means the rule tells you where to look rather than what the number is.
PracticeBefore handing a task over, write down what counts as a good result and what would have to be held steady around it; if either cannot be written, keep the task and hand over a narrower piece of it.

What gets automated depends on how controlled the setting is, not on how hard the task looks supported

Deciding exactly what to build is the hardest part and no tool or skill fixes a wrong choice supported
