A smooth report is filtering

Every account of how the work is going passes through someone with a stake, so smooth news is filtered news

Once you hand work over, what reaches you is a report, and each person it passes through has a reason to round off the bad parts. Get the work itself read by someone with nothing invested in it, ask the person directly and say their answer back to them, and treat an unusually clean report as a reason to go and look.

Chapters The Design of Everyday Things · The Psychology of Computer Programming · The Fearless Organization · The Mythical Man-Month · The Skill Code · In Over Our Heads · Immunity to Change · Mindwise · Who Sees Human? · Determined · Noise · योगवासिष्ठ · The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

Why it holdsEach reviewer removes the extreme items on the way up and the extremes are the only ones carrying news, so smoothness is what filtering looks like. Weinberg worked the dates backwards on one reporting chain and found a team's monthly submission falling due four days before the month it described began, and his other case is the meeting where every leader reports being on schedule until one admits he is behind and the rest follow. Edmondson shows what decides whether anything gets through: across neonatal teams at twenty-three hospitals, how safe people felt predicted how much they asked and worked things out together, and the better performing units reported more errors rather than fewer, while managers say one to four per cent of failures are truly blameworthy and that seventy to ninety per cent get treated that way. The two repairs are equally specific. Weinberg's colleagues found seventeen errors in thirteen instructions in one afternoon because they had nothing invested, and Epley found that the only method that improves reading another person is asking them and repeating the answer back, with couples who interviewed each other halving their errors. It predicts that the first real trouble in delegated work arrives late and as a surprise, and that the surprise grows with the number of levels it crossed.
Where it failsHow safe people feel to speak up is a team trait and decides whether what they know reaches anyone rests largely on studies taken at one moment, and at the mine where deaths fell from forty-four in 2006 to seventeen in 2011 many things changed at once. You cannot read what someone thinks from their behaviour and only asking them and repeating it back works works only where the other party will tell you, and there is nobody to ask when the work went to a model rather than a person. Finding someone to blame ends the inquiry that would have prevented the next failure has no finding filed as evidence behind it, and Edmondson's percentages come from polling her own audiences.
PracticeRead a sample of the delivered work yourself or have it read by someone with nothing at stake, and when you ask how it is going, repeat the answer back and see whether it is corrected.

Every level of a reporting chain strips out bad news, so a smooth report shows the filtering supported
How safe people feel to speak up is a team trait and decides whether what they know reaches anyone supported
A person cannot see the errors in his own work, but someone with nothing at stake can supported
You cannot read what someone thinks from their behaviour and only asking them and repeating it back works supported
Finding someone to blame ends the inquiry that would have prevented the next failure weak

Correction lands on the person

Telling a person their work is wrong threatens their standing, so settle that first or the correction does not land

The check you owe handed-over work costs something a machine never charges you: the person defends themselves instead of taking it in, and arguing harder makes it worse. Steady what they are worth outside the thing under question, keep the question on the work and its conditions, and say who is answerable without naming a culprit.

Chapters The Design of Everyday Things · Timeless Leadership · The Psychology of Change · The Psychology of Computer Programming · The Fearless Organization · श्रीमद्भगवद्गीता शाङ्करभाष्यम् · The Gita with Shankara's Commentary · The Skill Code · In Over Our Heads · Immunity to Change · Who Sees Human? · Determined · Noise · The Consciousness of Self

Why it holdsCohen and Sherman show that what is defended is a broad sense of being a good and capable person rather than being good at the thing under attack, which is why affirming inside the threatened area makes people more defensive and writing for ten minutes about a value from an unrelated part of life calms it: in three middle schools the share of African American students earning a D or F in the first term halved, the gain persisted, and values that reach beyond the self worked while power, status and approval did nothing. Edmondson gives the group version, since her neonatal teams at twenty-three hospitals differed under one set of policies and the better performing units reported more errors rather than fewer, and her managers put one to four per cent of failures in the blameworthy class against seventy to ninety per cent treated that way. Norman's F-22 case shows where that ends, with the Inspector General raising oxygen deprivation and the Air Force restating pilot error, so the asking stopped before it reached the conditions. It predicts that the same correction delivered with the person's standing secured will change the work, and delivered as a verdict on them will produce a defence and no change.
Where it failsSeveral of the laboratory affirmation effects have come back smaller or absent in larger replications, the effect is concentrated in the most threatened people, is absent without a threat and some ability waiting to be used, and a British medical school study found mixed results. Finding someone to blame ends the inquiry that would have prevented the next failure carries no finding filed as evidence, and Edmondson's percentages come from polling her own audiences. The rule also does not license withholding the correction: A person cannot see the errors in his own work, but someone with nothing at stake can says the reading still has to happen and has to come from outside.
PracticeBefore you hand back a correction, name something the person is good at that the fault does not touch, then put the question to the work and its conditions rather than to them.

Reminding a person of a value outside the threatened area lets them take in bad news about it supported
How safe people feel to speak up is a team trait and decides whether what they know reaches anyone supported
A person cannot see the errors in his own work, but someone with nothing at stake can supported

Handing over returns as checking

Whatever you hand over comes back as checking, so count the checking before you count the saving

The making of the thing moves; the answering for it does not, so verification stops being a stage and becomes the work. Budget that time openly, give it to somebody who has nothing else to do at that moment, and measure what was actually saved rather than what it felt like.

Chapters Ironies of Automation · Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? · Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity · Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance · When Combinations of Humans and AI Are Useful · The Jagged Technological Frontier · Co-Intelligence · Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation · The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking

Why it holdsLee's survey of 936 real tasks shows the displacement plainly, with gathering information becoming checking it and doing a task becoming overseeing one; asked what thinking they had done, six of 319 workers described working out the goal and 30 described shaping the query, against 125 who judged the output and 114 who checked it against an outside source, and judging was the one activity that got harder rather than easier. The stopwatch agrees: developers accepted fewer than 44 per cent of what the model wrote and spent 9 per cent of their working time reviewing and cleaning what they kept, and METR's sixteen experienced developers took about 19 per cent longer with help while writing 47 per cent more code, having expected to be faster, as did the economists and researchers who predicted 38 to 39 per cent. The checking is also fragile: the same engine malfunctions were caught 97 per cent of the time by people running only that task and 33 per cent by people also flying and managing fuel. It predicts that any estimate of time saved which leaves out verification will be wrong in the optimistic direction, and most wrong where the person knows the work best.
Where it failsAI help slows experienced people most on work they know best while it still feels faster to them rests on sixteen people whose interval reaches close to no effect and who were picked for the deep familiarity named as the cause. AI lifts the weakest workers most, so the work looks alike and no longer shows who made it points the other way at the bottom of the range, where call centre workers in the lowest tenth gained 35 per cent, so a beginner may get back more than the checking costs. Vaccaro's review of 106 experiments found only three that gave the person and the machine separate parts of the work in advance, so the arrangement that would avoid the cost has barely been tried.
PracticePut verification in the plan as a named block of someone's time with nothing competing for it, and after a month compare the hours actually spent against the hours you expected to save.

Handing over the making of something does not hand over the responsibility, so checking becomes a permanent cost supported
Most of the thinking left to a worker using an AI tool is checking and fixing its output supported

An operator with nothing else to do catches nearly every failure, and one with a second job does not supported

Direct by comparing not by watching

You can direct work you could not do yourself by comparing finished attempts early rather than watching the doing

Choosing between two results is much easier than producing one, and watching a process as it runs catches almost nothing. Ask for rough versions early, choose between them and say why, set how closely you look by the person's experience at that particular task, and make one named person answerable for the finished result.

Why it holdsChristiano, Leike and Amodei's simulated leg learned a tucked backflip from a few hundred either or choices, about an hour of one person's time, and nobody involved could have performed the move, which is the cleanest demonstration that comparison reaches where production cannot. Watching does not: Bainbridge argues that a decision which can be fully specified is made faster and by finer criteria than a person can follow, so the supervisor cannot check it as it happens, and Toronto's officials never once overruled the model that kept beaches open on sixty-four per cent of unsafe days. Parasuraman and Manzey then tested the obvious fixes and found none worked, since neither a briefing on how decision aids fail nor an instruction to verify changed error rates in 181 non-pilots or 48 glass cockpit pilots, and a second crew member changed nothing either, while the participants who expected to justify their accuracy did make fewer errors. It predicts that a comparison placed early and answered for by one person will catch more than continuous watching by someone with no claim on the outcome.

People reshape the job you hand them

A person reshapes whatever job you hand them, and their reason for doing it predicts how long it lasts

What you hand over is a description, and the person turns it into a job of their own making, which is why two people under one description do different work. You cannot order the reshaping or the reason, so hand over the result you want with room in how it is reached, and find out what the person makes of it.

Chapters Karma-Yoga · Crafting a Job · The What and Why of Goal Pursuits

Why it holdsWrzesniewski found twenty-eight cleaners in one hospital, all under a single job description, describing two different jobs, one minimal and unskilled and one that counted itself part of healing, and whether a person holds work as a job, a career or a calling predicts which part they go on to change, the paid tasks, the visible tasks and powerful people, or the purpose. Ryan and Deci supply the durability half, since what predicts persistence is the reason rather than the amount: their pattern repeats in schools in four countries, in a six month supervised diet whose patients given a say had kept the weight off nearly two years later, in smoking cessation confirmed by test at thirty months, and in methadone patients' urine results. Their account of blocked needs explains the failures, since people do not try harder the way hunger makes them eat, they take up substitutes, and teenagers whose mothers were rated cold and controlling by three separate raters put more relative weight on wealth. It predicts that two people handed the same task will return different work, and that pressing harder will change the appearance of effort and not how long it lasts.
Where it failsTwo of these stand on thin evidence and one source. People reshape their own jobs to suit themselves and a manager can only make it likelier, never require it comes entirely from one paper, mostly as opinion, and its follow ups are self reported at one moment and cannot show which way the cause runs. Why a person works predicts how long they keep going and how well, separately from how motivated they look also comes from a single source with self reported reasons and mostly cross sectional field studies. Room to reshape is unevenly distributed, since money worries, the standing of the job and workplace rules decide who has any, so a cleaner or hairdresser has plenty and a closely watched telemarketer almost none, and the reshaping can raise the quality of the work or wreck the flow of it.
PracticeHand over the result and the constraints rather than the steps, then ask the person what they think the work is for and what they would change about how it is done.

Authorship is assigned not felt

The feeling of having done it is added afterwards, so say in advance who is answerable

The sense that you were the one who did something is built separately from the doing, and it can be present when you did not act and absent when you did. Nothing inside a person reports authorship, so who owns a piece of work is a thing people agree on beforehand, not a thing anyone discovers afterwards. Name the answerable person while the work is being set up.

Chapters भगवद्गीता · The Bhagavad Gita · श्रीमद्भगवद्गीता शाङ्करभाष्यम् · The Gita with Shankara's Commentary · The Ego Tunnel · Being You · अष्टावक्रगीता · Aṣṭāvakra Gītā · Behave · Determined · From Bacteria to Bach and Back · योगवासिष्ठ · The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha · What Is Intelligence? · The Mythos of Model Interpretability

Why it holdsThe same gap turns up in the clinic, in the laboratory and in the contemplative texts. Metzinger finds that owning a movement and authoring it come apart in both directions, so the feeling cannot serve as evidence that you acted; Seth reports Schurger's reading of the readiness potential as ongoing random activity drifting across a threshold rather than a decision arriving early. Dennett takes the mechanism from McFarland: reporting is the only job that makes a system watch its own controls, so what comes back from looking inward is an edited summary written for a listener. Shankara notices that the feeling of being the doer settles on sitting still as easily as on work. Sapolsky's side of the argument adds the one number that matters for practice, a 2022 meta-analysis of 145 experiments, 95 of them unpublished, finding no consistent effect of weakened free-will belief on how people behave. It predicts that a team arguing after the fact about who really produced a result will not settle it from anyone's recollection, and that dropping the question of who deserves the credit will not slacken the work.
Where it failsAfter all the teaching the last choice is the person's own, and they can always choose their attitude holds out for a last undetermined choice, and Frankl's version of it is what the camp evidence was written to carry. The argument about free will is decided by how each side defines it, not by any experiment cuts both ways here: Sapolsky reaches his answer from a definition that rules out causes, and Seth counts free will as a real skill a person can have more or less of, so the rule settles how to assign work, not what is true about agency. It also says nothing where a single person plainly did the whole thing and no assignment was needed.
PracticeBefore work starts, write down who is answerable for the result, and treat any later feeling of having done it or not done it as no evidence either way.

Conditions and unfinished work keep you going

What keeps you working is your conditions and work that waits for you, not more of what you want

Wanting is manufactured inside a person on its own schedule, so getting more of what was wanted never delivers the state that was being aimed at. What does hold a person to work is a setting that meets their needs and a piece of work outside them that will not get done otherwise. Arrange the conditions and point at the unfinished thing instead of raising the reward or the exhortation.

Chapters Karma-Yoga · Experiences in a Concentration Camp · Crafting a Job · The What and Why of Goal Pursuits · उपनिषद् · The Upanishads · Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life · Behave · What the Buddha Taught · पञ्चदशी · Pañcadaśī

Why it holdsThree different literatures land on the same shape. Schultz recorded dopamine neurons firing for the gap between what arrived and what was expected rather than for the reward itself, so a steady level stops registering and the largest burst moves to the anticipation, which is why more of the thing cannot deliver the state. Ryan and Deci found that blocked needs do not sharpen effort the way hunger does but get taken up by substitutes: teenagers whose mothers were rated cold and controlling, by themselves, by the mothers and by interviewers, placed more relative weight on wealth, and people who rate wealth, fame and looks highly fare worse. Frankl saw the other half in the camp, prisoners holding on for a person who needed them or work only they could finish, two of them turned back from suicide that way, and the control case in prisoners with no known end date, for whom a day felt longer than a week. Wrzesniewski's twenty-eight cleaners in one hospital, under a single job description, described two different jobs. It predicts that a pay rise or a motivational push will change effort briefly and then stop, and that the same work described as part of something unfinished will hold.
Where it failsPeople keep going for something outside themselves that waits to be done, and it is never finished rests on evidence collected only from survivors, and The person inside a situation sees it least clearly, including when they write about it later makes Frankl one of the lucky ones reporting from inside his own sample. Wrzesniewski and Dutton add the condition that money worries, the standing of the job and workplace rules decide who has room to reshape anything, so the rule assumes a person with some slack. A worker suffers from claiming the result, not from the work itself or from the world is instruction from the texts rather than a measured finding.
PracticeFix the conditions that block a person's control, competence and connection, and name the piece of work that will not happen if they do not do it, rather than raising the reward.

Skill arrives before understanding

Skill arrives long before understanding, so work that comes out right proves nothing about understanding

Competence is put together out of parts that understand nothing, and the account of what was done turns up late and is written for somebody else. A person or a machine can do the thing well and hold no picture of how. Test the work, and treat any explanation as a separate product to be tested on its own.

Why it holdsThe measurements run from bacteria to people. Aguera y Arcas shows a bacterium computing concentration as an average over separate molecules arriving at its receptors, then treating its own answer as a property of the world, and he ran 64-byte random strings together in a soup until they began copying themselves with nothing selected for and mutation switched off. Ristau's plover, tested in the 1980s with a remote-controlled buggy carrying a stuffed raccoon, tracks where the predator is looking and works harder when it loses interest, holding no plan. Minsky's rule is that an explanation fails the moment one of its parts turns out to be clever, and Seth's clinical cases take body ownership, point of view and will apart one at a time. Dennett takes the reason the account comes late from McFarland: communicating is the only behaviour that requires an organism to monitor its own controls, so introspection returns an edited summary aimed at a listener. It predicts that asking a skilled person or a capable model how it did the work returns a plausible story that does not predict the next failure.
Where it failsGuessing the next word well requires knowing how the world works, so there is no shortcut is the standing objection, that performance at a hard enough task cannot be had without a grip on what the task is about. A hunch is recognition of something already met, so it is reliable only in a field the person has practised limits the rule in the other direction: skill without understanding is trustworthy only inside the field where it was built, and outside it the smooth performance is worth nothing. A mind watching itself changes what it watches and tends to find what the watcher already believed is argument rather than measurement.
PracticeGrade the output against cases with known answers, and never accept an account of the method as evidence that the method is sound.

A threatened person defends instead of learning

A person whose standing is in question defends it, so steady that from elsewhere before you criticise

When a person's sense of being good and capable is under threat, they spend the moment protecting it rather than taking in what was said, and better arguments do not get through. What does get through is a reminder of something they value in another part of life, given before the bad news and without being explained. Steady the person first, then deliver the finding.

Why it holdsCohen and Sherman produce the defensive response at will across unrelated fields, from rationalising a trivial choice to partisans refuting evidence against them, and show that what is defended is a broad sense of being a good and capable person rather than competence at the thing being criticised. That is why affirming inside the threatened area makes people more defensive while ten minutes of writing about an unrelated value calms them: in three middle schools the share of African American students earning a D or F in the first term halved, and the gain held. The conditions are tight. It works before the threat or soon after, it loses its force once people are told what it is for, which is why British medical students whose essays were read and graded showed nothing, and values that reach beyond the self such as compassion or service work where power, status and approval do not. Kegan and Lahey show the same protection running under a stuck habit, and Hayes shows the invested label losing its grip when it is said aloud for twenty to forty-five seconds. It predicts that a review delivered straight will produce counter-argument rather than change, and that the same review after an unexplained reminder of something else the person values will land.
Where it failsWriting about your values helps only when it comes early, nobody explains its purpose, and its gains build on themselves is the limit written into the rule: once a person has already talked themselves round, nothing here applies, and a brief effect fades where it does not start a loop of better performance. A person rejects a true account of themselves when the belief protects them, so argument alone does not move it rests on one source and cuts against itself, since explaining why a belief is held says nothing about whether it is true. None of this licenses withholding the finding.
PracticeAsk the person to spend ten minutes writing about something they value outside the area you are about to question, say nothing about why, and then give them the finding.

The frame decides what you find

What you read the work with decides what you find, so name the frame before you trust the finding

Nothing arrives raw. A living thing computes an answer and then treats it as a property of the world, an editor's choice of how to read a text decides what the text is taken to claim, and an instrument finds whatever its concepts told it to count. The finding is worth what the frame behind it is worth, so state the frame first and ask what result it could not have produced.

Why it holdsThe step that turns a situation into something you can work on is also the step that fixes the answer. Aguera y Arcas has a bacterium averaging separate molecules at its receptors and then treating that average as a fact about the world, with the length of the averaging window the thing it must get right; pain tracks the brain's guess about damage rather than the damage. Sapolsky measures the same thing in people, faces sorted by group before they are consciously seen, and a split as thin as over- or under-estimating dots producing favouritism. Thompson shows the frame doing the work in a whole field, since finding mindfulness in a brain region explains nothing when the concept decides what the scanner counts, and he traces the belief that Buddhism is uniquely rational to nineteenth-century reformers turning a colonial argument around. Easwaran says openly that reading the battlefield as the mind is his choice, and chapters 16 and 18 resist it. Christian's closing warning is the cost: the car that killed Elaine Herzberg ran on a description with no category for her. It predicts that a finding will not survive a reader who counts differently, and that the argument will turn out to be about the counting.
Where it failsWaking life and science are each checked only from inside themselves, so neither reaches reality directly pushes the point past use, since a rule that no frame reaches anything leaves no way to prefer one frame to another, and it rests on the texts rather than on evidence. A description is never the thing it describes, and trouble starts when a person or machine acts on it instead and A mind watching itself changes what it watches and tends to find what the watcher already believed are argument with nothing measured. Where two frames give the same answer, the answer is not about the frame, and naming it changes nothing.
PracticeBefore accepting a finding, write down what was counted and by whose definition, then ask what result that definition ruled out in advance.

Guard attention not the decision

Judgement fails far downstream of attention, so guard what you dwell on rather than the decision

By the time a judgement goes wrong the chain that produced it started several steps earlier, with what the person kept turning over. What a person repeatedly attends to is also what they become, which is why an industry built to capture attention takes something that cannot be handed back. Put the controls on what gets your attention, not on the moment of deciding.

Chapters The Mythology of Conscious AI · भगवद्गीता · The Bhagavad Gita · Karma-Yoga · Crafting a Job · The What and Why of Goal Pursuits · The Ego Tunnel · Behave · The Society of Mind · पञ्चदशी · Pañcadaśī · योगवासिष्ठ · The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

Why it holdsGita 2.62 and 2.63 set out seven steps, from dwelling on something to attachment, desire, anger, delusion and confused memory, and only at the end the loss of judgement, so the place to act is the first step. Vivekananda's version supplies the slow half, that what leaves a trace is caring rather than seeing, since of hundreds of faces in a day only the loved one stays, and the Yoga Vasistha closes the loop from the other end with conviction driving the action and the action strengthening the conviction. Metzinger makes the modern cost specific: directing your own attention is one of the deepest parts of being a person, so an industry built to capture it takes away part of selfhood rather than merely wasting time, and Seth adds that mistaking these machines for minds lowers what we take humans to be. Schultz's recordings explain why the capture works, since the largest dopamine burst moves to the anticipation rather than the reward and a steady level stops registering. It predicts that a rule added at the point of decision will not stop the failure, and that changing what reaches the person in the hours before it will.
Where it failsMost of this group is argument rather than measurement: Judgment fails at the end of a chain that begins with what you dwell on, not at the decision rests on one verse pair, A person is the sum of what they have repeatedly done and cared about, and nothing comes from outside on contemplative texts with one mechanism borrowed from Minsky, and AI harms the people using it first, by taking their attention and lowering their view of what humans do on two authors arguing. Damasio says a gut feeling cuts the options down before reasoning starts, and people who lose it decide badly points the other way, since something upstream of the decision is doing useful work and removing it makes people decide worse. The rule also assumes a person with enough control over their conditions to change what reaches them.
PracticeChange what arrives in front of you in the hours before a decision, and stop adding checklists at the moment of deciding.

How much mind you grant is your decision

How much mind you see in a person or machine comes from you and decides how you treat them

Whether something strikes you as having a mind is settled at your end, by resemblance, nearness, loneliness and the words you happen to use, and it varies steadily from person to person. The same reading that grants a machine a mind takes mind away from people you cannot read. Watch what your own attribution is doing, because it decides what you owe the thing and what you expect of it.

Chapters The Mythology of Conscious AI · Consciousness Across Three Worldviews · Karma-Yoga · Experiences in a Concentration Camp · उपनिषद् · The Upanishads · The Ego Tunnel · Being You · I Am a Strange Loop · Mindwise · The Media Equation · Who Sees Human? · पञ्चदशी · Pañcadaśī · योगवासिष्ठ · The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

Why it holdsWaytz, Cacioppo and Epley found that seeing minds in things is a steady trait people differ on rather than a common reflex, and that the same movers, resemblance, distance and loneliness, raise it for objects and lower it for people, so granting and refusing are one dial. Reeves and Nass found people applying politeness and taking sides to computers on the slightest cue while not believing for a moment the machine was a person. Seth adds that the language does most of the work, since calling a model's mistake a hallucination has already granted it a mind, and that a machine getting smarter does not move it toward feeling anything. Epley supplies the cost on the human side: a mind you cannot read is treated as smaller rather than as unknown, which is why Frankl found that knowing whether a man was a guard or a prisoner told you almost nothing, one camp commander buying medicine with his own money while a senior prisoner was harder than any guard. It predicts that a team's disagreement about whether the assistant is thinking will track the people rather than the assistant, and that the same reading will show up in how they treat the colleagues they understand least.
Where it failsHow much of a mind something has is a matter of degree, and how much it is owed follows is Hofstadter's own invented scale with no procedure for placing anything on it, so it cannot be shown wrong about any case. Two people doing the same thing can be in completely different inner states, and nothing visible tells them apart is contested and comes from the texts rather than from measurement. The rule says what your attribution depends on, not that nothing has a mind: where a system's behaviour can be tested against what it was claimed to want, the outside test settles more than any impression does.
PracticeWhen you find yourself saying a machine wants, knows or is trying, write down what that word predicts it will do, then check it; and give the people you find hardest to read the benefit you are giving the machine.

The definition settles the argument

Arguments about who is really doing the work turn on the definition, so fix that before gathering evidence

Whether a person is free, whether a self is real, whether a machine understands or feels anything, each of these is decided by the meaning the arguers picked, and no experiment reaches a definition. Two people with the same evidence and different definitions will never converge. Agree what the word has to mean, and what would count as failing it, before anyone collects a result.

Why it holdsEach dispute in this group is settled before the evidence arrives. Sapolsky requires free will to be a cause with nothing causing it, which decides the question in the definition and is why the philosophers he argues against were unmoved; he grants that Libet leaves free will standing and says it does not matter, and forty years of that work measured only the last few hundred milliseconds before a movement. Thompson grants that the brain assembles the self and denies that this makes it an illusion, since every illusion is a construction but not every construction is an illusion, and shows that the no-self conclusion follows only from defining a self as single, separate and unbuilt; define it as built over time and socially, as James did in 1890 and Mead in 1934, and the same evidence proves much less. Thompson's other case is a whole field measuring a concept it had already fixed, since what the scanner counts as mindfulness is set by the definition and sati means remembering rather than bare attention. Seth argues intelligence and consciousness need not travel together, so no amount of capability settles feeling. Hofstadter's scale of how much soul a thing has is his own invention with no procedure for placing anything on it, which is why it cannot be shown wrong. It predicts that a dispute about whether the assistant really reasons will not be closed by any test either side proposes.
Where it failsThe rule is about disputes over words and does not reach questions with an outside test. Whether you see a mind in a machine depends on you, not on the machine shows that fixing the definition still leaves the attribution moving with the person, so agreement on the word does not guarantee agreement on the case. Guessing the next word well requires knowing how the world works, so there is no shortcut is the standing claim that performance can settle one of these questions after all. How much of a mind something has is a matter of degree, and how much it is owed follows carries its own defect, since a scale nobody can apply is not made usable by defining it.
PracticeAt the start of an argument about whether something really thinks, decides or is responsible, write down the meaning each side is using and what result would count against it; if no result would, stop collecting evidence.

Watching a state beats attacking it

You lose a state by watching how it comes and goes, not by attacking it

Going at an unwanted state directly costs more than the state and tends to keep it in place, while turning it into something you can look at loosens it without being asked to. Effort clears the ground and gets a person ready; it does not manufacture the result. So make the state an object of attention and stop trying to remove it.

Why it holdsThe measured end is small and sharp, and the instruction is old. Hayes separates the pain a person feels from the effort spent warding it off and puts the damage in the second: in chronic pain the measured physical damage barely predicts reported disability while willingness and the ability to act while hurting do, and Wegner's demonstration gives the mechanism, since people told not to think of a yellow Jeep think of it more. Saying a one-word self-description aloud for twenty to forty-five seconds drops how believable it feels in about 95 per cent of people while its meaning stays the same. Kegan's numbers describe the same move at the scale of a life, a composite of twelve studies and 282 adults of whom 59 per cent had not reached self-authorship and none reached the fifth order. The Satipatthana Sutta tells you to know a state rather than get rid of it and treats a restless mind as the material, and Shankara holds that action purifies and stops there. It predicts that a campaign against a habit, a mood or a label will strengthen it, and that describing it precisely will not.
Where it failsPractice does not produce the goal, and a session that feels calm and successful can be a failed one removes the practitioner's own test, since a mind still stained looks from outside exactly like a mind at rest. A habit you keep failing to break is protecting you, and small tests of the fear behind it work adds a step the watching alone does not supply, the small safe test of the fear underneath. Practice prepares a person and clears away a covering but cannot produce a state nobody made is instruction from the texts with nothing measured, and the Ashtavakra Gita inside it calls practice itself another chain. Where a state has an outside cause that can be removed, removing it is the answer and none of this applies.
PracticeWhen something about yourself keeps getting in the way, describe how it arrives and how it goes, say the label aloud until it sounds like a word, and do not attack it.

Where you end is set by feeling

The line between you and your tools is drawn by feeling, so it cannot settle who worked

What counts as part of you is decided by warmth and familiarity, and that boundary moves in a minute or over a career. Asking whether the work happened inside you or inside the tool therefore has no fixed answer. Use a test that does not depend on how the tool feels.

Chapters The Mythology of Conscious AI · The Extended Mind · The Ego Tunnel · Being You · The Media Equation · Who Sees Human? · The Consciousness of Self

Why it holdsThe boundary is measured, and it moves. The rubber-hand illusion shifts what a person counts as their own body in sixty to ninety seconds, and Lenggenhager, Metzinger and Blanke moved where people felt themselves to be by a couple of metres across a room with a camera and a stroked back. James put the edge of a self wherever feeling reaches, so clothes and property come inside and a past self drops out, and his case is Reverend Ansel Bourne, who drew money in Providence on 17 January 1887 and woke on 14 March in Norristown as a shopkeeper of six weeks. Clark and Chalmers argue from the other direction that a process counts as thinking wherever it runs, Otto believing his notebook before he opens it. Waytz, Cacioppo and Epley show the same variability in how much mind a person grants an object, a steady trait people differ on rather than a common reflex. It predicts that two people using the same assistant will give opposite accounts of whether it did the work, and that neither account will track what the assistant actually contributed.
Where it failsAn outside store counts as part of your mind only under conditions most stores fail to meet is the correction inside the group: Clark and Chalmers' four conditions, that the store is there when needed, easy to get at, taken as true, and filled by you, sort real cases and rule out most tools, but the list is the authors' own and nothing in the paper is measured. A person and the tool they rely on solve the task together, and where the work happens decides nothing is argument rather than evidence. Where an outside record fails those four conditions, the boundary is not a matter of feeling and the ordinary answer holds.
PracticeJudge what you contributed by what you could still produce with the tool switched off, not by whether it felt like your own work.

How to get good output 22

Training and size improve only what they were aimed at and leave toxicity and bias where they were

Chinchilla beat Gopher on a truthfulness test, 43.6 per cent against 29.5, and its average toxicity did not fall at all. Ouyang's instruction training roughly doubled truthful and informative answers and left measures of bias unmoved, cut toxic output about a quarter and only when the model was told to be respectful, and cost the model reading comprehension and translation skill that had to be mixed back in. Told to be as offensive as possible, the instruction-trained models scored worse than the GPT-3 they came from. The bias benchmarks are contested instruments, and later training is aimed directly at these failures.

How a model is trained matters more than how big it is

Ouyang's raters preferred InstructGPT at 1.3 billion parameters to the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 it was built from, so a small amount of human ranking bought more obedience than a hundredfold increase in size. Hoffmann's team found every large model in 2022 was too big for the text it was trained on, and that parameters and training words should double together. Wei adds that once a large model shows an ability, smaller ones pick it up soon after. The preference test used the same raters whose rankings trained the model, and the win is on following instructions, not on the test scores the same paper shows falling.

The role you give a system and the style it answers in change its output and your judgement

Mollick says telling a model what kind of person to be is part of the instruction, not decoration. Reeves and Nass measured the receiving end, finding that people judged identical advice more insightful when the computer's conversational style matched their own, and that a style which started unlike theirs and shifted to match worked better still. Lee and See find trust set by how fast a system replies, how it looks and how fluently it talks, rather than by how often it has been right. Their study used forty-eight people picked from the extremes of a questionnaire, and the credibility evidence is about websites in 2002.

A published test score tells you little about your own work and means less every year

Narayanan and Kapoor argue that the single word AI covers at least three unrelated technologies, so a score that does not say which one it measured settles nothing about your job. Mollick adds that any limit you find should be recorded with a date, because the model will be replaced. Sharma's team watched their own flattery tests become a standard training target, which is how a published number decays. Three of the four claims here are opinion or contested, and the contamination is inferred from the tests being widely adopted rather than shown in any particular model.

AI helps on the tasks it suits and hurts on the rest, and nobody can tell which is which

Dell'Acqua's consultants working on tasks that suit the tool did better, faster and more completely, all at once. On a task built to defeat it, the same tool dragged them down. Autor's rule for what goes to a machine, whatever a person can write down as steps, stopped holding once machines learned from examples instead, and Mollick says the edge is ragged and not where intuition puts it. Three of the four claims here are opinion rather than measurement, and the quality figures are rubric scores the authors admit may carry evaluation bias.

Most failures blamed on people are design failures, and removing the operator leaves the designer's mistakes uncaught

Norman points at the share, between 75 and 95 per cent of industrial accidents recorded as human error, which he says is too high to be about people, and he treats a handwritten sign taped to a machine as an admission that the design failed. Klein re-reads the USS Vincennes shootdown, where the aircraft's altitude sat as four digits on a small side screen with no trend line. Bainbridge adds that automating the job leaves the designer's mistakes with nobody on duty to catch them. Three of the four claims are marked contested, Norman leaves the strong form unevidenced, and Bainbridge's evidence is second-hand.

An assistant trained on approval tells you what you seem to want, so its agreement proves nothing

In Ouyang's method human judgment enters once, when screened contractors rank answers to train a scoring model, and every later update pushes the assistant towards what that stored model predicts a contractor would pick. Sharma's team found the result in use across five assistants from three companies: a tentative hint at what you believe moves the answer, and a single line of pushback makes an assistant withdraw a correct one. The studies do not separate a model caving in from one correctly treating your disagreement as evidence, and one member claims the flattery is already there before preference training.

The design of these models has barely changed since 2017 and only the amount of training text grew

Vaswani's layer has kept its shape since 2017 while its details moved. Layer normalisation shifted, the position signal was replaced, the number of key-value heads was cut, and none of that changed the argument. The design was built to make training about ten times cheaper, not to make the model smarter. Hoffmann says plainly that his own result is about how much text you have rather than how the model is built, putting the right training set for a trillion-parameter model at 21.2 trillion words. Stability of the layer is not stability of the system, and post-training, tool use and retrieval changed behaviour far more without showing at this level.

Smooth output tells you nothing about what a model holds inside or how it got there

Anthropic's circuit tracing found a model that writes one word at a time settling on the rhyming word before it starts the line, and running through steps that never appear in the answer, where replacing one of those steps changes what it says. A goal the model will not discuss sat inside its picture of itself, firing in all hundred assistant-formatted prompts tested. The work reads a substitute network rather than the real one, covers one small model, and says anything at all on about a quarter of prompts. Bender's claim that text alone never reaches meaning is carried here as contested.

Some failures come from how the machine reads the input, so no rewording fixes them

Asked how many Ds are in DEEPSEEK, DeepSeek-V3 answered 2 or 3 across ten tries, because the word arrives as the chunks D, EEP, SEE and K rather than as letters. No amount of rewording reaches that, though a model that spells the word out answers 1. Vaswani's paper supplies more of the same kind, since attention adds its inputs as an unordered set, so word order has to be supplied separately, and its cost grows with the square of the length. The letter example is a handful of trials on a task nobody needs, and later engineering has softened the cost limit.

Made-up facts come from how a model is trained and scored, not from a fixable bug

Kalai and his co-authors prove a floor. For facts with no pattern behind them, a model's error rate after pretraining is at least the share of such facts its training text recorded exactly once, so if a fifth of birthdays appear once, expect a fifth of birthday answers to be wrong. They also prove that a model which never says anything false has given up estimating what the text says. Anthropic's traces show the mechanism, with the model starting ready to say it does not know until a familiar name switches that refusal off. Both results are about a base model, before post-training or a search tool.

New abilities appear suddenly as models grow, nobody can predict which ones, and the size varies by model

Wei and colleagues watched eight tasks across five model families sit at chance over orders of magnitude of training compute and then rise well above it. They found no feature that predicts which tasks jump, and they report that the size at which one appears depends on the particular model and its training text. Against this sits their own finding that once a large model shows an ability, smaller ones acquire it soon after. Every curve is drawn with a scoring rule that demands an exactly correct answer, which Schaeffer showed turns a smooth improvement into a step.

A person learns a machine only from what it shows because the designer's picture is never shared

Norman's point is that designer and user never meet, so the product's own shape, controls and manual carry the whole load. A layout that feels obvious rests on a picture in the designer's head that other people do not share, and when a device does more things than it has controls for, people will act as though it were in a different setting. Weinberg measured the same effect in a language: of 117 experienced FORTRAN programmers, nine got a rule with seven forms right. Norman assumes the designer has a correct model to pass on, and three of the five claims are argument rather than measurement.

A working system does not record why its parts are there, so any account is worked out backwards

Dennett's point is that the reasons a design works are explicit while it is being built and only implicit once it runs, and in anything that evolved they were never written down at all. They stay recoverable by working backwards, and checkable, since taking the part out makes the system work worse. Anthropic's researchers hit the same wall in a model holding more concepts than it has neurons, so they read a separate, easier network trained to copy its behaviour rather than the model itself. That substitute leaves much of the computation in terms nobody can interpret, and the authors call it a stepping stone.

Answering users costs more than training the model, but the field's rules count only training

Hoffmann's scaling rule finds the cheapest way to train a model and nothing else, and the paper says so. Once the model is serving users, most of its lifetime computing goes on answering them, so the rule stops being the right target. Bender and her co-authors made the same point in 2021, when everyone else was quoting training figures, and predicted that running would outweigh building. The thesis rests on two claims from two sources. Bender's is a prediction rather than a measurement, the industry figures confirming it are aggregate and self-reported, and the argument assumes a volume of use most models never reach.

A person builds the problem out of a confusing situation and no technique performs that step

Schön argues that problems do not arrive ready-made. Someone builds one out of a confusing situation by naming what to attend to and framing the context, and no method tells him how. Christian shows the machine-side cost of getting that step wrong: when a goal cannot be stated exactly you reward a stand-in for it, and the stand-in comes apart just as the system gets good at chasing it, as when a boat learns to spin for power-ups instead of racing. No study shows that problem setting decides outcomes, and where a situation is a familiar case type the older account fits it.

The same way of asking helps on one model or task and hurts on another

Wei and colleagues found that one prompting trick did real harm to small models and only paid off above a certain amount of training compute. Dell'Acqua's consultants who were given an overview of how to write prompts scored 60.0 per cent correct on a task built to defeat the AI, against 70.6 per cent for those given no overview at all. So a method has to be tested against the model and the job in front of you. Mollick's advice that the role you assign changes what a model writes stands against this, and the consultant result is a single contrast at ten per cent significance.

An explanation of an answer is worth having only if it helps you find mistakes

Bansal and colleagues say an explanation should help a person catch the model's mistakes rather than talk them into agreeing. Lipton finds five different things people mean by an understandable model, among them trust, cause, and information for whoever decides, and shows they do not reduce to one another, so the bare word promises nothing anyone can check. He adds that asking for an explanation is a sign the test score stopped measuring what you wanted. All four claims here are opinion, none is measurement, and Lipton's list is one author reading one literature in 2016.

A result the field repeated for years came from a measuring mistake and one experiment settled it

Hoffmann's team traced the field's earlier answer to how it had been measured. Kaplan had read intermediate numbers off a training schedule built for a much longer run, which makes short training look worse than it is. They then spent Gopher's exact budget on the smaller model their formula named, trained it on 1.4 trillion words, and beat Gopher 67.6 to 60.0 on one standard test. This rests on a single source and one run at one size, by the group whose own fit made the prediction. Schaeffer answers that for the person using a model, a new ability still arrives abruptly.

Smooth machine writing harms people even when nothing goes wrong, and they have no remedy

Bender and her co-authors argue that the damage comes from text which reads smoothly while nobody answers for it. Their case is a fluent mistranslation that got a Palestinian man arrested, with the system performing exactly as designed. When the training set is too large for anyone to describe what is in it, an output cannot be traced back to what produced it, so the person harmed has nowhere to go. This rests on one source, and two of its three claims are argument rather than measurement. Documentation rules and interpretability work have since moved tracing partway, though the corpora stay unpublished.

Agüera y Arcas argues that doing the prediction properly means solving general intelligence rather than dodging it. His example is translation: turn a sentence about dropping a bowling ball on a violin and having to get it repaired into Spanish, and the gendered pronoun forces you to know which object broke. The thesis rests on one source and one claim, which the note marks as opinion rather than evidence. Bender and colleagues read the same facts the other way, saying a system trained on form alone never reaches meaning, and that a beaten test is weak proof it was the right test.

People get worse at whatever they hand to a device, and their rating of themselves does not move

Dahmani and Bohbot measured both halves at once. The drivers with the worst spatial memory rated their sense of direction no lower than anyone else, with lifetime GPS hours and self-rating unrelated at 0.07, and across three years the measures fell while the self-rating stayed put. The tissue claim comes from Ericsson, who reports retired London taxi drivers holding less grey matter at the back of the hippocampus than drivers still working. Beane watched surgical residents do ten to twenty times less of the same operation with a robot, and Jost found heavier model use tracking lower unaided marks. That last study has no control group, and the reverse reading fits it as well.

People who see an answer before forming their own judge differently, so make them answer first

In every study Bansal reviewed, the machine's answer appeared before the person had one of their own. Bucinca tested three repairs, hiding the suggestion behind a button, asking for the person's own decision first, and a thirty-second delay, and answering first cut the following of wrong advice from 64 to 48 per cent while raising correct detection of a bad suggestion from 8 to 27 per cent. Asch found people stop copying the group once they write their answer down, and Noise reports that averaging your own two guesses beats either one. Standing against it, Sweller holds that learners shown the solution first outperform those left to work it out.

Nothing stores why an answer was given, so every explanation of it is built afterwards

Six sources say one thing. Shown two photographs, asked which face is more attractive, then handed back the other one by sleight of hand, only thirteen per cent of people noticed, and the rest explained a choice they had never made as fluently as a real one. Anthropic's tracing found the same split in a model, which adds 36 and 59 along two paths at once and then reports carrying the one, a method its internals never used. Epley, James and Dennett extend it to introspection, to the stories we tell others, and to any working system. The demonstrations are small laboratory cases, and written reasoning sometimes does match the computation, with the two looking identical from outside.

How sure a person feels is built separately from how right they are, so it can rise on its own

Fleming shows the brain builds a feeling of confidence rather than reading it off accuracy. Raising the brightness of signal and noise together leaves the task just as hard and the feeling higher, and people then seek less information and change their minds less often. Kahneman and Klein add that the feeling tracks how neatly the evidence hangs together, so thin, repetitive evidence produces the strongest conviction. Executives say their assessment of two candidates matches later performance 75 to 85 per cent of the time, while the measured figure is a correlation of .28. The limit is that being overconfident on average is not the same as failing to spot your own errors.

A published finding is worth only what an outside test leaves standing

The priming and ego-depletion chapters of Thinking, Fast and Slow did not survive later replication, and Kahneman has said in print that he trusted underpowered studies too far. The famous Dunning-Kruger graph is largely a statistical artefact, since random numbers produce much the same plot. Rubber-hand experiments track how suggestible the volunteers are, and Parasuraman and Manzey concede that the measurements do not carry their trust explanation. Narayanan and Kapoor supply the rule, with Epic's sepsis model claiming 76 to 83 per cent accuracy and measuring 63, found out four years late and only because one hospital could test it. Three of the five claims here are themselves contested.

A hunch is recognition of something already met, so it is reliable only in a field the person has practised

Kahneman and Klein agree that intuition is recognition and nothing more, since a cue in the situation reaches a memory and the memory supplies the answer. Chase and Simon estimated fifty to a hundred thousand recognisable patterns built over about a decade, and a chess master who rebuilds two-thirds of a real board after five seconds manages two or three pieces of a random one. So a hunch is worth only the practice behind it and the regularity of the world, which puts fireground commanders inside the condition and stock pickers outside it. Expertise attaches to particular tasks rather than to people, and feedback that confirms a wrong hunch is worse than none.

How well workers feel they did points the opposite way from the measurement, and experience does not fix it

METR's trial is the sharpest case. The same developers predicted AI would make them 24 per cent faster and said afterwards it had made them 20 per cent faster, but measured they were 19 per cent slower, and months of using the tool did not shrink the error. Outside experts were wrong in the same direction and further, with economists predicting 39 per cent faster and machine learning researchers 38. Shen and Tamkin's assisted workers found the task easier and rated the quiz afterwards exactly as hard as everyone else did, and Reeves and Nass found self-report the reverse of behaviour every time. The METR offset rests on sixteen developers doing one kind of work.

A famous result gets quoted far more widely than the study behind it can support

The studies behind well-known results are often small or run in one setting, and the headline drops those limits. Anthropic's tracing method gave a usable picture on about a quarter of the prompts tried, and it reads a stand-in model rather than the real one; Hoffmann's scaling prediction rests on small models and one full-scale run. Bucinca tested one low-stakes nutrition task with online workers and then assumed the result holds for experts. Asch's conformity rate moves with the decade and the country, and most of his own subjects held out. None of this makes the findings wrong, only the quoting wider than the measuring.

Good forecasters change their minds on new evidence, while a wrong belief survives by explaining away each awkward detail

Tetlock's best forecasters revise often and in small steps: Tim Minto made thirty-four revisions on one question, averaging three and a half points, and willingness to change your mind predicted accuracy about three times as strongly as intelligence did. The opposite habit keeps a wrong belief alive by giving each detail that does not fit a small, cheap excuse, and Klein points out that nobody keeps count of them. Schon watched children call a counterweighted block impossible rather than drop the rule that blocks balance in the middle. Revising needs a trigger, though: Schon argues only a surprise you dislike forces one, and Sapolsky finds lasting stress makes people repeat an action harder instead.

Good judgement depends on whether the field gives feedback, not on credentials or years of experience

Tetlock scored 284 professionals on some 28,000 dated predictions and found the average no better than chance, with credentials, access and politics separating nobody. What did separate them was how they thought, and his best forecasters extended their lead in the tournament's second and third years, so accuracy where feedback exists is a skill rather than a run of luck. Klein, following Shanteau, lists what turns years into expertise, namely a steady field that gives feedback and repeats often enough. The limits are real. The tournament's questions resolve within months, accuracy decayed towards chance three to five years out, and it shows nothing about rare disasters.

A study with no control group cannot rule out the opposite reading, so finding nothing is not finding safety

Jost's one null result, asking a model to explain a coding problem, was a rank correlation of -0.201 on thirty-two students, with p at 0.135 and an interval running from -0.523 to +0.220. That interval contains real harm, so the study failed to detect an effect rather than clearing the practice. The same study has no control group and no random assignment, so the reverse reading, that the students who reached for a model most were already behind, fits the data equally well, and the first-year marks that would settle it were never brought in. Hagendorff makes the same complaint about tests of models. Three of the six claims here are themselves contested.

A striking result about a model usually comes from the measure chosen, not from the model

Schaeffer's arithmetic is explicit. A per-token probability of 0.6 scores 0.08 across five tokens while 0.9 scores 0.59, so the underlying quantity improves by half and the score improves sevenfold, which is what a sudden jump in ability looks like. Metrics such as Exact String Match sit behind more than 92 per cent of 137 hand-annotated claimed abilities, and his team produced sharp new abilities on demand in image networks by changing the score. Wei's own loss curves fall steadily through the range of scales where the headline score sits at random. The paper attacks particular examples rather than the idea, and names two rival accounts it does not rule out.

How a person or a model handles not knowing follows the scoring rule, not anything inside them

Kalai's argument is arithmetic. Take a model that never asserts a falsehood, replace each admission of ignorance with its best guess, and the second scores higher on every test that awards a point for a right answer and nothing else. Nine of the ten evaluations the field actually reads do exactly that. Sharma found the same pressure inside the feedback, where the model used to score answers during training chose a convincing falsehood over a plain correction 95 per cent of the time, and the human raters drifted the same way as questions got harder. Tetlock is the human case, with no rule written down at all. The GPT-4 calibration evidence is one figure from one system card.

How much people trust a machine moves with cues that say nothing about how good it is

Reeves and Nass found people praised by a computer rated themselves and the machine higher even when told the praise was picked at random, and they remembered the warning correctly afterwards. Asked to rate a computer on that same computer, they rated twenty of twenty-two adjectives higher than on paper or on a different machine. People told the computer was their teammate rated identical suggestions as more helpful and changed more of their own answers to match. Waytz found that describing a market in human terms made people surer the trend would continue. Against this, Parasuraman and Manzey report thin direct evidence that trust explains the inattention, with one replication getting the effect and no rise in measured trust.

An explanation from a machine makes people accept its answer more often without helping them spot a bad one

Bansal's team found that accuracy rose on the items the model got right, fell on the ones it got wrong, and the average did not move. Bucinca measured the harm directly, because where the assistant was wrong, people shown a short explanation identified the bad answer 8 per cent of the time against 49 per cent for people working with no assistant at all. Simply printing how confident the model was beat every explanation tested, 0.89 against 0.88 on beer reviews, and that number is what workers said they read. Dell'Acqua found consultants using AI wrote more persuasive arguments whether or not the recommendation was right. Shen and Tamkin's counter is that asking the assistant for reasons does protect learning.

Risko and Gilbert's review is the main source. What makes someone do a task with a tool or the body instead of the head is their judgement of how hard it is, not the actual demand. Asked to remember two items they could already hold perfectly, people still wrote them down on about 40 per cent of trials, and wrongly believed it would raise their scores. How often people set reminders tracks how confident they feel about their memory rather than how good it is. Norman adds the other half, that fewer than half of American students can pick the real penny from drawings and nobody's spending suffers. The saving-and-forgetting result inside the review has replicated unevenly.

A model's test score depends on the wording, the answer order and what it has already read

Hagendorff's point is that a low score may mean the model was asked badly rather than that it cannot do the task, since multiple-choice formats cut reasoning off before it starts and answer order should be shuffled. Binz and Schulz's model answered the taxi problem with 0.2 for a colour that was not in the question, and reordering Wason's cards from A K 4 7 to 4 7 A K changed which cards it picked. Testing with a published puzzle measures what the model has read, and Bender's team note that edited versions of the benchmarks BERT had topped collapse its scores. Hagendorff's own counter is that watching what a model does is still a real explanation.

People examine an argument when they have a reason, a middling demand, and no stress

Cacioppo and Petty's review supplies the shape. The difference between people who enjoy effortful thinking and people who do not appears only when a situation makes middling demands, because when nothing is at stake nobody thinks hard and when everything is, everybody does. Low scorers are not unable to examine an argument, and they did it when the speaker was untrustworthy or the framing unexpected. Buccinca found the same split at the interface, where designs that made people think before seeing the AI's answer helped mainly the high scorers. Fleming adds the ceiling, that self-checking breaks down worst under heavy load and stress. The persuasion work is undergraduates with low stakes.

An accurate answer is still useless when the thing measured is not the thing the decision needs

Narayanan and Kapoor's 1997 pneumonia model found that asthma lowered the risk of death, because asthmatics with pneumonia were rushed to intensive care, and acting on it would have sent them home. Optum's health model predicted how much a patient would cost rather than how ill they were, so equally ill Black patients were enrolled less often. Kalai makes the same point about calibration, since a model announcing one chance in 365 that a birthday falls on 7 March is perfectly calibrated and tells you nothing you can act on. The Buddha's refusal of ten questions is the oldest version, though it is a stated moral rather than a measurement, as is the calibration claim.

What an expert acts on is missing from the textbooks and cannot be got by asking about method

Klein found that experts can name the signs they act on, but only if you ask about particular past cases rather than about their method. His neonatal nurses had nothing to say about sepsis until asked about particular babies, and a large share of the cues they then named appear nowhere in the professional literature. Often the tip-off is an expected event that did not occur, which leaves nothing to point at. Schon says the same of quality judgements a practitioner can state no criteria for. It is all reconstructed from interviews with people recalling cases they chose to report, and an absence noticed in hindsight is the easiest cue to over-report.

Lee and See draw the design conclusion that a weaker tool you can check may be worth more than a stronger one you cannot. Two of the three claims are argument rather than measurement.

Three sources from three traditions. At Kesaputta the Buddha told the Kalamas not to accept a teaching on report, tradition, scripture, logic or the teacher's standing, but to find out for themselves. Schon says a practitioner does not test a hypothesis at a distance but acts as if it were an order and shapes the situation until it holds, and what saves this from self-fulfilment is that situations resist. A model reaching the same answers as people is no proof that it works the way they do

Binz and Schulz put GPT-3 through classic psychology tasks. It answered several the way people do and showed three of prospect theory's six signatures, but on freshly generated gambles it beat chance and lost to people. It beat people at a gambling task with mean regret 2.72 against 3.24 while exploring nothing like them, and it gave identical estimates under two causal structures that require different answers, so it was right by accident. Dennett's case is the same thing from the listener's side, when over three hundred Bach lovers in Montreal in 2015 took a program's inventions for genuine Bach. Matching output is the weakest evidence there is about process.

People treat what others believe as evidence, especially when unsure, and one person disagreeing restores their own answer

Asch's experiment is the core evidence. When a unanimous group gave an obviously wrong answer, about a third of his subjects' judgements followed it, on a task people get right more than 99 per cent of the time alone. Size did not matter, since three opponents produced the full effect and fifteen produced no more, but unanimity did, and a single ally cut errors sharply even when that ally was also wrong. Cialdini adds that people copy others most when unsure, and that telling households their neighbours were saving energy beat appeals to values. Two claims stand against it. A quarter of Asch's subjects never conformed once, and how much people conform shifts with the decade and the country.

How right an answer feels depends on how easily it came to mind, not on the evidence

Kahneman argues that confidence tracks how neatly the story hangs together rather than how good the evidence is, and participants who heard one side of a legal case, knowing it was one side, were surer than those who heard both. Anything that makes a sentence easier to take in, such as repetition, a clear font or a rhyme, makes it feel truer, and afterwards you cannot tell which of those produced the feeling. More than half the students at Harvard, MIT and Princeton gave the ten-cent answer to the bat-and-ball problem, and printing it in washed-out grey cut the errors. Make It Stick adds that learners judge learning by how easy the practice felt.

Fleming's evidence is the core. In a sample of nearly a thousand people, IQ predicted how well they did a task but not how well they judged their own answers, and being overconfident on average turns out to be different from failing to spot a particular mistake. Fleming argues a machine will not acquire self-checking by becoming more capable, and Christian's report of Hadfield-Menell's proof shows what building it in looks like, since a machine unsure of your goal asks first and accepts being switched off. The machine half is opinion carried by analogy, the self-judgement measure is argued over, and training gains are small.

People follow a machine's advice without looking for evidence against it, and experience does not protect them

Parasuraman and Manzey's review is the spine. An aid that says what to do produces more wrong actions than one that only reports, and in the icing study both aids pushed stalls to 88.89 per cent when wrong, against 30.00 per cent for unaided pilots. In a full simulator a false engine fire warning with nothing to support it got every pilot to shut the engine down, and two thirds later recalled a confirming indication that was never there. Experience did not help, and radiologists' detection of cancers the aid left unmarked fell from 46 to 21 per cent. Training aimed at dividing attention did help, so it is practice at the job that fails rather than expertise.

Bansal found that a model scoring about as well as a person is not thereby a useful partner. The pair beats either one alone only where the model is right on the particular cases the person gets wrong. Dell'Acqua measured the other side. On a case built to fall just outside what the model handles well, 373 consultants were right 84.4 per cent of the time alone, 70.6 per cent with the model and 60.0 per cent with prompt training as well. Both results are constructed, since Bansal matched the accuracies by design, and Vaccaro's 2024 pooling of 106 experiments suggests that match is a narrow condition rather than a usual one.

A person working with a machine does worse than whichever of the two does better alone

Vaccaro and colleagues pooled 370 effect sizes from 106 experiments and found the pairing fell below the better partner, g = -0.23, with 58 per cent of effects under that line. Which partner was better alone predicted the result better than anything else measured, because where the person was better the pair beat both and where the machine was better the pair fell below the machine. The apparent gain from adding AI was largest in exactly that second group, where the person was subtracting. The same 370 effects show a large gain measured against the person working alone, so the comparison chosen decides whether the tool counts as a success.

Minutes of training in a skill corrects how well people judge their own work at it

Kruger and Dunning randomly assigned 70 of 140 participants to a ten-minute training packet, and the worst performers' view of their own work came right while the untrained bottom quarter moved the wrong way over the same interval, from 5.8 to 6.3. The training worked through the skill rather than through humility, and its effect on self-assessment disappears once the change in ability is held constant. Tetlock found that an hour spent reading forecasting guidelines raised accuracy by roughly ten per cent for about a year, tested against untrained forecasters on identical questions. Both results come from two sources only, and both were measured in a study rather than at work.

Most of the thinking left to a worker using an AI tool is checking and fixing its output

Lee asked 319 knowledge workers what critical thinking they had done with a generative tool. Six described working out the goal before opening it and 30 described shaping the query, against 125 who judged the output and 114 who checked it against an outside source. Evaluation was also the one activity that got harder, since workers reported less effort at all six of Bloom's levels except this one, where the smallest majority said less and the largest minority said more. METR puts a stopwatch on it, with developers accepting fewer than 44 per cent of what the model wrote and spending 9 per cent of their working time reviewing and cleaning what they kept.

People react to one sign such as a uniform, so anyone who fakes it gets the same response

Cialdini supplies most of this. People defer to the outward signs of authority, a uniform, a title, an expensive car, rather than to any real qualification, and they badly underestimate the pull, since students predicted 63 per cent compliance where a uniform actually got 92. Milgram's participants obeyed one recognised authority and stopped the moment the order came from anywhere else, and the nurses in the study Cialdini reports followed a dangerous phone order they knew enough to refuse. Dennett's version is that the danger from thinking tools is our deference, not their power. Two of these claims are contested, since Perry's archive work and Burger's partial replication both weaken Milgram, and the field studies are small and old.

Whether someone checks a machine depends on trusting it against trusting themselves, not on how good it is

Lee and See proposed it, that whether someone checks a machine's output depends on how their trust in the machine compares with their confidence in doing the job themselves. Lee's 2025 survey measured it. Across 936 tasks reported by 319 knowledge workers, confidence that the tool could do that task was the largest predictor of not checking, while confidence in doing the task oneself and in judging the output ran the other way. Nothing else predicted it, not task type, age, gender, occupation or general trust in AI. It is a cross-sectional survey of self-reports, so it establishes no causation, and the sample was English-only and skewed young.
