A person told to supervise a machine cannot catch its errors

Bainbridge argues that when a decision can be fully specified the computer makes it faster and by finer criteria than a person can, so the operator cannot check it as it happens and nothing settles who wins a disagreement. Attention on a quiet display fails after about half an hour, which the vigilance work going back to Mackworth in 1950 measured. Manual operators arrive a quarter to half an hour early to build a picture of the plant, and someone taking over from automatic control has had none of that. Dell'Acqua adds that nothing announced which of the tasks fell outside the model's range. Two of the four claims are argument rather than measurement.

A simple rule built from an expert's own past decisions beats the expert by answering the same way every time

The formula uses no information the expert did not have. Goldberg's models tracked their judge at about .80 across 237 studies and lost no accuracy replacing them, and in one replication ninety-eight people predicted ninety students' grades from ten cues with the model of each participant beating that participant every time. Grove's meta-analysis of 136 comparisons puts most of the margin down to consistency alone rather than better information, and no study has shown an expert catching a strong clue the formula missed. The formula also subtracts the expert's subtle rules along with the noise, and it assumes the cues are already chosen and quantified, which is most of real judgment.

An expert recognises what kind of situation this is, and the action comes with the recognition

Klein interviewed experienced fire commanders under time pressure and found they do not weigh options against each other. They recognise the kind of situation they are in, and the action to take arrives with the recognition, tested if at all by imagining that one option play out and watching for what goes wrong. Dreyfus puts it as skill growing by dropping rules rather than collecting them. Three of the five claims here are contested. The interviews were coded by the researchers who ran them, Klein's count of about three moving parts has never been replicated, and his 2009 settlement with Kahneman narrows all of it to fields with valid cues and a fair chance to learn them.

An explanation built to satisfy people is aimed at sounding right, not at showing where the model is wrong

An account extracted from a trained model afterwards costs no accuracy and says nothing about how the model works, so an opaque system supplies one as readily as a clear one. Lipton's sharpest case is Krening's second model, trained to produce verbal accounts of a reinforcement learner by fitting the explanations human players gave, which need not describe the agent's decisions however plausible it sounds. Saliency maps hold only around one image, and Adebayo showed in 2018 that several widely used methods produce much the same map after a model's weights are randomised. Vaccaro's meta-analysis of more than 300 effect sizes found neither explanations nor confidence scores improved teamwork. Lipton's half is argument rather than measurement.

An operator with nothing else to do catches nearly every failure, and one with a second job does not

In the 1993 experiment the same engine malfunctions were caught about 97 per cent of the time by people running only that task, and 33 per cent by people also flying and managing fuel by hand. Parasuraman, Molloy and Singh ran three tasks at once and found detection averaged 82 per cent when the automation's reliability fluctuated against 33 per cent when it held constant. Lee and See report the same split, replicated with experienced pilots and with rare faults, and found that ten minutes of manual control brought detection back up. The cause here is competing load rather than trust, which matters because the remedy differs. Only two claims support it, both from the same literature.

The errors that do damage look like correct work and come from steps done without attention

Norman separates a slip, the right intention carried out wrongly at the late steps of acting, from a mistake, which is the wrong intention formed while planning. Experts slip more often, precisely because practised action runs without conscious attention. Mollick supplies the machine version, that the errors which do damage are the small plausible ones surviving a careful reading, and his own three paragraphs about the Schwartz case, written with web access, were wrong in three small ways. This is the thinnest of these theses, two sources sharing a mechanism but not a subject, and Mollick's case is a single demonstration on one passage.

The same expert judging the same case twice gives two different answers

A professional is not the same measuring instrument on two occasions. Wine judges scored 18 per cent of the same wines identically on a second tasting, software developers estimating the same task on two days differed by 71 per cent, and opioids were prescribed more often late in the day across nearly seven hundred thousand primary care visits. Two underwriters at one insurer, pricing the same file, differed by a median of 55 per cent, against the 10 per cent their executives had predicted. Sapolsky adds that the frontal cortex tires first, so timing shifts judgement, but that mechanism is listed as contested and controlling sleep and time of day does not drain the spread.

Duley laid the automated engine display over the manual tracking task, so that every look at the tracking task also fell on the automated one, and tracking stayed as good as before while the rate of missed malfunctions did too. In the same review about 43 per cent of operators missed a first wrong diagnosis, and half of those had looked at every reading and spent no extra time on the one that did not fit. A little learning makes people confident, and more of the same learning makes them worse

Tetlock found that hedgehogs, experts who explain everything through one big idea, forecast less accurately inside their own specialty than outside it. More information poured through a single lens buys confidence and no extra truth. The Upanishads say the same without measurement, since the Katha warns not against ignorance but against the confidence of a little learning, describing the blind led by the blind and denying that reasoning alone settles the question. Two claims and two sources, one of them contemplative and unscoreable. Klein's evidence runs the other way where cues are valid and feedback is fast, and neither source tells you which sort of field you are standing in.

A paper's famous conclusion often survives after the method behind it fails

Two cases carry this. Of the three methods Hoffmann used, the one that leaned hardest on fitting the data did not survive a later re-check, while the conclusion the paper is remembered for did, and the correction moved that third route into agreement with the other two. Damasio's broad position, that emotion sits inside reasoning rather than outside it, is now the standard view, but the bodily-marker machinery he built it on has thinned as criticism of his card game accumulated. Two claims and two sources is thin, one of them contested, and the audit worked from published figures rather than the original data.

A tool weakens the skill it replaces while the person's own estimate of that skill stays put

Risko and Gilbert's model has two arrows, one from offloading to the skill and one from offloading to the judgement of the skill, so reliance grows with nothing in the person's own report registering the loss. Turn-by-turn navigation makes the journey better and the driver worse. People who searched online about one subject credited themselves with more knowledge of a different subject, a transfer that only an inflated self-estimate explains. Shen and Tamkin found the group using an AI assistant fell furthest behind on debugging questions, which is the fault-finding that checking a tool needs. That breakdown was exploratory rather than planned, and two of the four claims are contested.

Outsiders can only learn what a model does by testing it, and words like wants must predict what it does

Hagendorff argues that studying what a model does when you use it is a proper explanation, because its outputs cannot be predicted from what is known about its weights, and for a closed commercial model it is the only route open to outsiders. He also defends describing a model as believing or wanting something, on the grounds that such words explain its behaviour better than a mechanical account even when nothing inside matches them. Binz and Schulz supply the evidence that the method outlasts the score, since their GPT-3 result was stale within a year while the design survived. Against it stands the finding that a single phrasing measures nothing, because answers shift with wording and position.

People do not use information just because someone puts it in front of them

Two studies sit behind this. Dennett reports that people told not to use a briefly flashed word obey when the word is shown for half a second, but at fifty milliseconds and masked they say they saw nothing and are more likely to give that very word. Buccinca and colleagues find the same thing at the screen, where people read an AI's explanation as a sign the machine knows its job rather than reading the explanation itself, which is why a better explanation does not produce a better decision. That second half is inferred from the pattern of results rather than observed, and a 2023 study found explanations do cut over-reliance where checking is cheaper than deferring.

The first number or starting point a judge sees moves the final answer without them noticing

Two claims sit here. Kahneman's is that people judge an outcome as a gain or a loss measured from a starting point rather than as a level of wealth, and that a loss feels about twice as heavy as a gain of the same size. Tetlock turns the same fact into a working order, to ask how often such things happen in general before looking at the particular case, because whichever number you meet first is where your estimate settles. Neither half is strong alone. Tetlock's ordering has never been tested against the reverse, and the endowment effect that follows from Kahneman's kink does not appear among experienced traders.

The more reliable a machine is, the less people watch it, and small checks are the practice

Parasuraman and Manzey describe the loop. Automation is usually reliable, so watching it less usually costs nothing, and the absence of a cost makes the operator watch less still. Only an experienced failure reverses it, and operators who met rare failures in training sampled the aid more than operators merely told it might fail. Lee's survey supplies the second half, where 55 of 319 knowledge workers said a task was too trivial to be worth checking and only 13 checked anything in order to keep a skill, so the consequential tasks arrive unrehearsed. The loop itself is borrowed from other work rather than measured, and nothing in Lee's single snapshot shows judgement actually decaying.

A mind cannot watch itself working, so the verdict on its own judgment has to come from outside

Minsky's argument is mechanical. A programmer debugging a program stops it first, and a brain running many processes at once cannot, because freezing one changes what you were studying and freezing all of them hides the interaction. The Yoga Vasistha makes the same point from the other end, when Vyasa's son Suka has worked the truth out alone and cannot call it finished until king Janaka hands the same conclusion back in one sentence. Both members are opinion rather than measurement, one an argument from how hardware differs from brains and the other a single invented case with its moral supplied, which is why the note counts as weak.

Damasio says a gut feeling cuts the options down before reasoning starts, and people who lose it decide badly

A feeling attached to an imagined outcome arrives before the options are weighed, and it drops most of them. Damasio's patient Elliot scored superior or average on every intelligence test and still spent half an hour listing reasons for and against two appointment dates without choosing. Eleven further patients with the same prefrontal damage showed the same pairing of lost feeling and lost judgement, and healthy card players sweat before a risky deck while these patients do not. The general point was accepted but the particular mechanism was not; several of the card-game results have been reassigned since, and that dispute is the claim standing against.

Whoever lacks the skill to get an answer right also lacks the skill to see it is wrong

Kruger and Dunning ran the studies this rests on. Across humour, logic and grammar their bottom-quarter students placed themselves at or above the middle, a 12th-percentile performance rated at the 62nd, and asked about raw scores rather than rank they claimed 14.2 of 20 logic items against an actual 9.6. The same students could not tell good work from bad in other people's answers, so watching better performers taught them nothing. The support is weak, since it is one source, and the crossing-lines graph everyone remembers can be produced by regression to the mean plus the general tendency to rate oneself above average. The rest of the evidence survives that criticism.

Trying harder to read another person raises your confidence but not your accuracy

Epley's evidence is that confidence in reading another mind far outruns accuracy, and that longer acquaintance raises only the confidence. Dating partners predicted each other's answers 44 per cent of the time and believed they had got 82 per cent right. Imagining yourself in someone's position does not help and can hurt, because it runs your own mind inside a stereotype. People who switched to the method that halved their errors felt no more confident than before, so confidence cannot tell you which method is working. Support is weak at one source, and the accuracies are modest rather than zero, so the gap is the finding rather than a failure of mind reading.

Beyond competence people improve by reorganising what they know rather than adding rules, and courses cannot take them there

Past the stage the Dreyfus brothers call competence, a learner stops collecting rules and starts responding to whole situations, and that cannot be handed over in a course. Klein's fireground study is the strongest number: of 156 decision points from non-routine incidents, 127 were recognitional and only 18 involved comparing options, and half the comparisons came from one fire staffed by novices. Papert's conservation result makes the same point about children, whose largest step adds no new skill, only a better way of managing old ones. Three of the nine claims are contested and Klein's is also filed against. Sweller keeps explicit instruction all the way up, with randomised trials behind him.

Support that helps a beginner starts to hurt an expert, because what helps depends on what you already know

Difficulty is a relation between the material and the reader rather than a property of the page, so the same help changes sign as knowledge grows. Sweller's expertise reversal effect, named in 2003, is the replicated result: worked examples and other supports stop being necessary and then start to hurt. The mechanism is that working memory holds only a few new items but an unlimited amount of what is already familiar, which is why Chase and Simon's chess master replaces two-thirds of a real position after five seconds and two or three pieces of a random one. The reversal is established for lessons in well-structured subjects, and extending it to a tool used for years is an extrapolation.

Handing over the making of something does not hand over the responsibility, so checking becomes a permanent cost

The work of producing the thing moves to the machine and the answering for it does not, so verification stops being a stage and becomes the job. Lee's survey of 936 real tasks found the displacement plainly: gathering information became checking it, and doing a task became overseeing one. Vaccaro's review of 106 experiments found only three that gave the person and the machine separate parts of the work in advance, so nobody has really tested the alternative. Bansal's table adds that in all eight studies offered as evidence for explanations, the model alone beat the human-machine team. Lee's counts are self-reports and cannot be netted against each other.

Oversight written into a process goes unused and only being answerable for the result changes what people check

A rule saying a person may overrule the system does not make them do it. Toronto's officials never once overruled the model that kept beaches open on sixty-four per cent of unsafe days. Parasuraman and Manzey tested the obvious fixes and found nothing worked: neither a briefing on how decision aids fail nor an instruction to verify changed error rates in 181 non-pilots or 48 glass-cockpit pilots, and a second crew member changed nothing either. Only participants who expected to justify their accuracy made fewer errors. That accountability was explaining yourself to an experimenter, and Edmondson finds accountability without safety produces silence rather than checking.

Finding someone to blame ends the inquiry that would have prevented the next failure

Naming a culprit answers the question the investigation was asking, so the asking stops before it reaches the conditions that produced the failure. Norman's case is the 2010 F-22 crash, where the Inspector General raised oxygen deprivation and the Air Force restated pilot error. Edmondson shows the size of the habit: managers say one to four per cent of their organisation's failures are truly blameworthy, and that seventy to ninety per cent get treated that way. None of the four claims counts as evidence, and Edmondson's figures come from polling her own audiences rather than from records. Norman adds that asking why implies one cause where complex events have many.

A tool that lets experts work without juniors removes the work that made juniors able to check it

The machine does not take the expert's job, it makes the junior optional, and the junior's work was how competence got built. Beane watched ninety-four operations across five hospitals: residents did surgical work for almost the whole of an open procedure and ten to twenty times less of a robotic one, where the surgeon sits alone at a console. Mollick makes the same point about entry-level work in law and software. All eight claims lean one way and none is filed against, but the evidence is one speciality, observed rather than randomised. Beane's bomb-disposal teams, who put the controller in a trainee's hands, show that deployment decides this and not the machine.

How safe people feel to speak up is a team trait and decides whether what they know reaches anyone

Two teams in one company, under the same policies, can differ sharply, so the unit that matters is the group rather than the person or the firm. Edmondson's study of neonatal teams at twenty-three hospitals shows the mechanism: how safe people felt predicted how much they asked and worked things out together, and had no relationship at all with how much they read on their own. Her better-performing hospital units reported more errors, not fewer. At Rustenburg mine, where explaining had produced silence, a change to open questions came alongside a fall in deaths from forty-four in 2006 to seventeen in 2011. Much of this literature is cross-sectional, and many things changed at Rustenburg at once.

Changing how a group decides works where training its people to be less biased does not

You cannot train the bias out of a person, and Kahneman says decades of study left his own judgement as overconfident as before, but you can change what the group has to do. Noise supplies the strongest number: American sentencing guidelines cut the expected gap between two judges from 4.9 months to 3.9, and after the Supreme Court struck them down the penalty for drawing a harsh judge doubled and the racial gap widened. Premortems and reference-class forecasting work the same way. The guidelines were repealed anyway, which is the honest limit, and the debiasing failure is Kahneman's concession rather than a trial.

The way of working that feels harder while you do it teaches you more

Ease during practice and learning afterwards run in opposite directions, so the feeling is a bad guide to what is working. Ninety per cent of students did better after spaced practice while seventy-two per cent said cramming worked better for them. Roediger and Karpicke found recall beat re-reading, sixty-eight per cent against fifty-four at two days, with the study-only group forgetting half of what it could first recall against a tenth for the tested group. Bucinca extends it to AI advice, since making people answer first cut their following of wrong suggestions from sixty-four per cent to forty-eight. Sweller's result is filed against, and the rule does not mean any difficulty helps.

A tool that decides for you costs the ability it replaced and the loss shows only without it

Using a device that makes the decisions leaves nothing for the underlying skill to practise, so the skill fades where no ordinary measure looks. Dahmani and Bohbot tested fifty Montreal drivers: the more lifetime hours a person had spent under satellite navigation, the worse they did with no device at all, and thirteen retested three years later had declined in step with the hours logged in between. Jost made the same argument by design, marking students only on work done with the tools removed. The effects are small, the samples tiny, and the strongest follow-up rests on thirteen people. The retired-taxi-driver finding is filed against as well as for, since it measures brain volume and not navigation.

Automation keeps the routine work and leaves people the rare hard cases they no longer get to practise

The tasks nobody could write a specification for are the ones left to a person, and those are the rare and abnormal ones. Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation is the source: routine work is what keeps a manual skill alive, so an operator who has only watched for months performs like a beginner when control comes back, and the more reliable the system the more training its operators need. Lee and See add that people given other work alongside the watching miss most failures. Bainbridge's paper is a review that cites its studies a sentence each, and two of the seven claims are filed against, including Ericsson's.

The problems that matter lie where technique stops working and a finished demonstration hides the fumbling a learner needs

Schon divides practice into a high ground where technique works and a lowland of confusing messes it cannot solve, and puts the problems people care about in the second. His own case turns on him: Quist's studio demonstration is so accomplished that it corrects no errors and compresses out the iterations a student needs to see. Ross and Bagnell proved the machine version, where a learner given only clean demonstrations has no recoveries to copy and a million frames of expert play left the network crashing as often as two thousand had. Three of the seven claims are filed against, and Schon never says how to tell which ground you are standing on.

A stand-in measure stops matching the real goal once whoever is measured gets good at chasing it

Because the goal cannot be written down exactly, someone rewards a stand-in for it, and the stand-in comes apart from the goal just as the chase gets skilful. Christian's The Alignment Problem supplies the cases: a boat that spins in the harbour collecting power-ups instead of racing, a bicycle that rides twenty-metre circles because moving away from the target was never charged. Grove's answer is a second number beside every first one, and Ng and Russell proved an added bonus stays safe only when it depends on where the agent is. The cases are simulated agents, and carrying them over to people rests on a shared pattern rather than a shared mechanism.

A person cannot see the errors in his own work, but someone with nothing at stake can

Attachment to your own work hides its faults, so the reading has to come from someone with nothing invested in it. Weinberg's founding case is one afternoon of colleagues reading his code: seventeen errors in thirteen instructions, and no further error in nine years across a dozen installations. He claims the gain shows up as delivery dates that vary less rather than as work finishing faster. Beane adds that expertise narrows what anyone notices, since eighty-three per cent of radiologists hunting for lung nodules missed a picture of a gorilla forty-eight times larger. Only one of the four claims counts as evidence, and the gorilla is a search task rather than a professional judgement.

An automated decision can fail because the data or the rules are wrong, and no better model fixes that

Checking outputs catches a model that is wrong about the world. It cannot catch a model that is right about bad records, or a disagreement about where the rule should fall. Christian gives the cases: Caruana's pneumonia model learned that asthma patients were low risk, true in the data only because they went straight to intensive care, and dropping race from the inputs leaves it in through address and prior convictions while removing any way to measure it. Narayanan and Kapoor add that moderation fights are policy disputes people must settle. The pneumonia case is fifteen thousand patients from one era of medicine, and their account of why institutions buy what fails is assembled from examples rather than tested.

You cannot read what someone thinks from their behaviour and only asking them and repeating it back works

Watching someone and inferring what they think is unreliable, however confident it feels. Epley found the one method that improves it is asking the person and saying the answer back, and couples who interviewed each other halved their errors. His rigged quiz shows the failure, since the audience rated the question-setters at the eighty-second percentile and the contestants at the forty-ninth, and only the setters, who knew how many questions they had thrown away, rated the two sides equal. People also badly overstate group gaps, predicting thirty-five points where the measured party difference was 3.5. It works only where the other party will tell you, and there is nobody to ask when the delegate is a model.

Deciding exactly what to build is the hardest part and no tool or skill fixes a wrong choice

Brooks argues the hardest single part of building software is deciding exactly what it should do, and that clients cannot describe it correctly until they have used some version of it. Tools only ease the writing down, and his prediction that no one development would make software work ten times faster within a decade has now run four decades. Weinberg supplies the evidence from the other side, since his programmers did whatever the written instructions asked and a group told to finish fast produced programs about ten times slower. Hardest is never measured against anything, and Weinberg's experiment had four subjects in one shop and has not been repeated at scale.

What gets automated depends on how controlled the setting is, not on how hard the task looks

The same physical task falls on either side of the line depending on its surroundings. A car plant fits windscreens with robots, while replacing the same glass in a garage uses a technician, because removing a broken screen and preparing the frame demands adaptation no affordable robot manages. Amazon's Kiva robots automated the warehouse by moving shelves across a level floor while a person still does the picking. Minsky states it from the other side, since mathematical logic fell to a program in 1956 and college calculus in 1961 while what a four-year-old does resisted for decades. Both claims count as evidence, but the price of making a setting controlled is usually invisible and enormous.

Every level of a reporting chain strips out bad news, so a smooth report shows the filtering

Each reviewer removes the extreme items on the way up, and the extremes are the only ones carrying news, so smoothness is what filtering looks like. Weinberg worked the dates backwards on one reporting chain and found a team's monthly submission fell due four days before the month it described began. His other case is the meeting where every leader reports being on schedule until one admits he is behind and the rest follow. Brooks supplies the structural version, since half a project's time goes on testing and the slip surfaces only then. Of three claims one counts as evidence, and Brooks later withdrew the schedule model his rule sits inside.

When a job asks for a different kind of mind, training and new skills cannot supply it

Training works on what a mind holds, while some demands are about how it is organised, and adding skills leaves that untouched. Kegan and Lahey give a test anyone can run, that a behaviour returning after honest effort is doing a job for the person. Their case is Peter, whose ten pounds stayed off for four years while the softened tone he had worked on came back, plus seven per cent, against an average dieter who regains 107 per cent of what was lost. Two claims from two books carry the whole thesis. The test is also backward-looking, and Ericsson holds that much of what is called a difference in kind yields to structured practice.

What defeats adding people to a project is the cost of coordinating them, not their individual ability

Each person added has to be trained by those already working, and the talking grows faster than the headcount, so the work does not divide. Brooks states it flatly: adding people to a late software project makes it later. Weinberg's rule of thumb, that three programmers do about twice the work of one, points the same way, and his correction of the famous thirty-to-one gap between programmers, which came from comparing the best person on one task with the worst on another, supplies the other half. No claim here counts as evidence, three are opinion and two contested, and Weinberg's numbers are asserted rather than measured.

AI help slows experienced people most on work they know best while it still feels faster to them

Measured time and felt time move apart. In METR's randomised trial, sixteen experienced developers fixing real issues in codebases they had worked on for years took about nineteen per cent longer with AI help than without, while writing forty-seven per cent more code per hour, and the slowdown was largest where their own knowledge ran deepest. Economists and machine-learning researchers asked to predict the result guessed thirty-eight to thirty-nine per cent faster. Sixteen people is a thin base, the confidence interval reaches close to no effect, and the participants were picked for exactly the deep familiarity the authors name as the cause, which most work does not have.

Why a person works predicts how long they keep going and how well, separately from how motivated they look

Two people who look equally keen can be headed in different directions, because what predicts persistence is the reason rather than the amount. Ryan and Deci's pattern repeats across settings: schools in four countries, a six-month supervised diet whose autonomy-supported patients had kept the weight off nearly two years later, smoking cessation confirmed by biochemical test at thirty months, and methadone patients' urine results. Managers can be trained to give staff more say, and a Fortune 500 study found subordinates reporting the change over thirteen months. Everything here comes from one source, the reasons are self-reported, and most of the field studies are cross-sectional.

Computers cut middle-paying jobs and move work to both ends of the scale while pay does not follow

The jobs computers take sit in the middle of the pay scale, so employment grows at the top and the bottom, and the pay at the bottom does not rise with it. Autor's figures carry it: the four middle-skill American occupation groups fell from sixty per cent of employment in 1979 to forty-nine in 2007, and across sixteen European economies between 1993 and 2010 the middle-paying share fell in every single country. Real wages below roughly the fifteenth percentile fell between 1999 and 2007 even as those jobs grew. Both claims come from one author, so it stands on thin evidence, and a falling share is not a falling count.

A person can direct work they could not do themselves by comparing results instead of producing them

Judging between two finished attempts is easier than making one, so a person can push work toward what they want without being able to do it. The single claim behind this comes from Christian's The Alignment Problem: Christiano, Leike and Amodei's simulated leg learned a tucked backflip from a few hundred either-or choices, about an hour of one person's time, and nobody involved could have performed the move. One simulated robot carries the whole thesis, so it stands on thin evidence. The method also assumes the chooser knows what they want, and where all the choices were collected before training the agent kept the loopholes it found.

Automating part of a job makes the rest worth more only where demand grows and entry stays hard

A job is a bundle of tasks, so making the machine's tasks cheap can raise the price of those left to a person, but only under conditions. Autor names three: the worker supplies the remaining task, others cannot easily enter it, and demand for the output grows as it gets cheaper. His case is the cash machine, which rose from about 100,000 to 400,000 in America between 1995 and 2010 while bank tellers rose from about 500,000 to 550,000. His own wage series is the counter-case, and the point is contested: at the bottom of the scale real wages fell after 1999 even as those jobs grew.

A manager's real output is what his teams produce, so work that lifts nobody else counts for nothing

Andrew Grove measures a manager by what his group delivers, not by how busy or how able he looks. Every claim here comes from Grove's High Output Management: rate no manager above his team's actual result, run the training yourself rather than hiring a trainer, set targets people reach about half the time. Grove derived the rule from running Intel and never tested it. It is an accounting identity rather than a measurement, since it cannot split one result among several influences, and a manager's work may surface years later. Five of the six claims are opinion and one is contested, with nothing filed as evidence.

Practice prepares a person and clears away a covering but cannot produce a state nobody made

Effort can get a person ready and take away what is in the way, but it cannot manufacture something that was never made. Shankara argues that action purifies the mind and stops there, that knowing the Self uncovers it rather than gets it, and that only those who do not yet know have duties. The Ashtavakra Gita goes further and calls practice itself another chain, and Rahula says nirvana is not an effect of the path. Eleven claims from five contemplative sources, all opinion and nothing measured. Chatterjee stands against it, holding that letting go of being the doer can be trained by regular reflection.

What you meet is already interpreted, built from what you expected and one detail, and it changes with the setting

What reaches a person has already been worked on. Seth says you see the brain's best guess rather than the incoming signals, and Minsky says most of what you see is filled in from expectation and that what reaches awareness is a record of a moment already gone. Sapolsky supplies the evidence: faces are sorted by group before they are consciously seen, a split as thin as over- or under-estimating dots produces favouritism, and a hormone lowers a threshold rather than adding a behaviour, which is why an automatic reaction changes with the question asked. Eight claims from four sources, six of them evidence, none against.

A mind watching itself changes what it watches and tends to find what the watcher already believed

Thompson's objection is that meditation trains and alters the mind while it observes it, so it cannot be the neutral instrument the comparison with science needs — Nyanaponika claimed both that bare attention follows the true scientist's procedure and that it makes the mind more plastic. The Mandukya Karika reaches the same place from the other side, listing how each school looking for the self found its own founding principle, breath or the elements or the void. Easwaran's Upanishads and the Satipatthana discourse both give a procedure with no outside check. None of this is measured, and schools disagreeing is still consistent with one of them being right, an objection that applies to the texts making it.

Awareness is what everything is known by, and it stays through waking, dream and sleep while their contents drop out

Whoever does the knowing cannot be found among the things known, and these texts test that across waking, dream and sleep, where contents drop out and something stays to report. Two people doing the same thing can be in completely different inner states, and nothing visible tells them apart

Nothing on the outside separates two people doing the same thing in different inner states. The Panchadasi says flatly that in doing or leaving undone, in body, senses, mind or intellect, there is not the least difference between the man who has woken up and the man who has not, and that the difference is one of conviction only. Suraghu in the Yoga Vasistha says the lotus posture gives nothing and daily work prevents nothing, and Vivekananda says refusing to fight means nothing unless you could have fought. Against this stands Wrzesniewski, who measures the inner stance precisely by what people change in their behaviour.

You cannot tell from what a system does whether it feels anything, because being smart is not being conscious

Behaviour does not settle whether there is anything it is like to be the system. Seth argues intelligence and consciousness need not travel together, that making a machine smarter does not move it toward feeling, and that a simulated brain is conscious only if consciousness turns out to be computation, which he doubts because a brain has no software separate from its biology. Everything a person does has causes behind it, and people who drop blame for that reason do not behave worse

Every action has a history behind it, and letting go of blame on that ground does not make people worse. Sapolsky's Determined argues that randomness is not freedom, that chaos removes predictability without leaving anything free, and that willpower is brain tissue shaped by luck. The strongest number is a 2022 meta-analysis of 145 experiments, 95 of them unpublished, finding no consistent effect of weakened free-will belief on ethical behaviour, and society has twice dropped blame without falling apart. Two claims stand against: Sapolsky defines free will as a cause with no cause, which settles the argument before evidence arrives, and Seth counts free will as a real skill.

A person whose worth is under threat defends themselves instead of learning, and argument does not change that

Cohen and Sherman's review shows the defensive response produced at will across unrelated domains, from rationalising a trivial choice to partisans refuting contrary evidence, and shows what is being defended is a broad sense of being a good and capable person rather than being good at the thing under attack. That is why writing about a value from an unrelated part of life calms the threat while affirming inside the threatened domain makes it worse. Chatterjee and Shankara read the same pattern in Arjuna's collapse, and Krishna's reply replaces his way of seeing rather than arguing with it. Several of the laboratory effects have come back smaller or absent in larger replications, and Chatterjee's version is not falsifiable.

Wanting is produced inside you regardless of what arrives, so getting more of it never brings the state you wanted

Wanting runs on its own schedule, so more of what was wanted does not deliver the state the person was after. Schultz recorded dopamine neurons firing for the gap between what arrived and what was expected rather than for the reward, so a steady level stops registering and the biggest burst moves to the anticipation. Ryan and Deci report that people who rate wealth, fame and looks as important relative to other goals score lower on well-being, whatever their reasons. A mind is made of parts that are not minds, and no thinker or owner stands behind them

Minsky's rule is that an explanation fails the moment one of its parts turns out to be clever, and that an inner watcher only needs a watcher of its own. Rahula reaches the same conclusion from the Dhammapada, where the third line changes the word so that no thing at all, conditioned or not, is a self. Seth supplies the one piece of measured support, clinical cases in which body ownership, point of view, will, life story and social self fail separately — Clive Wearing keeps the first four and loses the thread. Motivation comes from a person's conditions, not from being told to try harder, and blocked needs produce substitutes

Ryan and Deci's finding is that blocked needs do not make people try harder the way hunger does: they take up substitutes. Teenagers whose mothers were rated cold and controlling by themselves, by the mothers and by interviewers placed more relative importance on wealth. Wrzesniewski and Dutton's model of why workers reshape their own jobs, for control, self-respect and connection, is assembled from adjacent literatures rather than tested, and they add that money worries, the standing of the job and workplace rules decide who has room to reshape anything. Vivekananda's version, that work from love leaves no painful reaction, has no outward sign and no count behind its ninety-nine in a hundred.

The story you tell about who you are does the damage, and it loosens when you treat it as words

Hayes argues that the self a person builds in words is the dangerous one, because once you are invested in a label you are invested in being right about it. The measured support is small and sharp: saying a one-word self-description aloud for twenty to forty-five seconds drops how believable it feels in about 95 per cent of people, while its meaning stays the same. Two older texts sort the attachments rather than the words — the Buddha's formula names craving, conceit and taking something to be a self, and the Drig-Drishya Viveka counts three identifications of which only one is an error. Believability is not behaviour, and the step from a rating to what someone does is not closed.

Your explanation of why you decided something is produced by a separate part built for telling other people

Dennett takes the mechanism from McFarland: communicating is the only behaviour that requires an organism to monitor its own control system, so looking inward returns an edited summary built for reporting, not a view of the machinery. Agüera y Arcas adds that the narrating voice is aimed at a listener, since you already know what you are thinking and they do not. Dunbar's measurements in the 1990s, cortex rising with group size and more steeply in apes than monkeys, are the only numbers here. A troop-size correlation fits several stories, and nothing offered separates this account from the simpler one that explaining yourself is just useful.

A person is the sum of what they have repeatedly done and cared about, and nothing comes from outside

Vivekananda holds that every action leaves a trace, that the traces add up to character, and that what leaves the trace is caring rather than seeing — of hundreds of faces in a day only the loved one stays. The Yoga Vasistha states the same loop from the other end, conviction driving the action and the action strengthening the conviction, with nothing stored in between. Minsky supplies the only mechanism, memory as switching back on whatever was active before. All four are arguments or images rather than measurements, the machinery around Minsky's version produced almost no experiments, and a loop with no outside cannot say how the first conviction got in.

Sarvapriyananda says the whole apparatus of witness, veil and three selves is a way of teaching rather than a list of things that exist, and reading it as a list is the error the texts warn against. The Drig-Drishya Viveka makes the point at verses 13 and 15, where what gets hidden is never the rope but its being a rope, so the appearance itself does no damage until a difference is forgotten. Easwaran's Upanishads and the Pañcadaśī are read the same way, as procedures with one part of ignorance producing the grief. All of it is illustration, and the move insulates the teaching, since anything that fails can be called method rather than doctrine.

Anything you can notice is not the one noticing, so awareness never shows up among the things it shows

Anything that can be noticed falls among the things shown, so whatever does the showing never appears there. Drig-Drishya Viveka argues that anything you can see is not the one seeing, that the body seems aware only because awareness is passed down a chain, and that anyone denying the witness is using it to deny it. Shankara puts pleasure and pain among things seen rather than with the seer, and the Ashtavakra Gita says you are not even the one who knows. Six claims from three contemplative sources, none of them evidence. James stands against, since for him the passing thought is the thinker and nothing stands behind it.

Grief comes from what you were told and from calling something mine, not from what happened in the world

The Pañcadaśī's pair does the work: a father whose son is alive abroad weeps at a liar's word that the boy is dead, while a father whose son has really died does not weep because the news has not reached him. The two differ only in what they were told. The Yoga Vasistha adds the second half, three fighters made without conditioning who could not be killed until the gods put the feelings of I and mine into them. Nothing is measured, both are constructed stories, and Vidyāraṇya blocks the idealist reading himself by saying the world in the mind still needs the outer one as its basis.

Waking life and science are each checked only from inside themselves, so neither reaches reality directly

Nothing checks waking except more waking, and nothing checks science except whether it works for people like us. Gaudapada's Mandukya Karika argues that waking is worth no more than dreaming and that a thing missing before and after is missing in between. The Yoga Vasistha's King Lavana shuts his eyes in court for under an hour and comes out having lived seven years, so felt duration measures nothing outside itself. Thompson pushes the same move onto science. All five claims are opinion or contested, from three sources with no evidence, and Thompson's step is disputed and hard to hold without losing the ground to state it.

Your nature does the act and the feeling of having chosen it is added afterwards, even when you sit still

The act happens first and the sense that you chose it is added afterwards. Easwaran's Gita says nature does the deed and the ego claims it, Shankara points out that the feeling of being the doer arrives over sitting still just as readily as over work, and the Ashtavakra Gita's free man keeps acting while feeling no authorship. Five claims from three contemplative texts, three opinion and two contested, none of them measured. The weak point sits inside the group: if the sense of authorship goes and behaviour does not change, nothing outside the person separates this from ordinary idleness.

Skill comes before understanding, and understanding is a late product of a process that has none

Dennett's case is that design fills the living world without anyone understanding anything, so skill comes first and understanding arrives late. Ristau's plover, tested in the 1980s with a remote-controlled buggy carrying a stuffed raccoon, tracks where the predator is looking and performs harder when it loses interest, without holding the plan. Agüera y Arcas ran 64-byte random strings together in a soup and after millions of interactions they began copying themselves, with nothing selected for and mutation switched off. All four supporting claims carry measurements rather than argument. Against them stands the argument that predicting the next word well requires knowing how the world works.

A living thing works out what it senses and then treats its own answer as a fact about the world

An organism does not read properties off the world. It computes an answer and then treats that answer as a property of what it sensed. Aguera y Arcas shows a bacterium working out concentration as an average over separate molecules arriving at its receptors, with the length of the averaging window the thing it has to get right, and pain tracking the brain's guess about damage rather than the damage. Dennett adds that there is no sweetness in glucose, only properties that provoke a response, and the response is read back into the sugar. Three evidence claims from two sources with none against, but the range runs only from a bacterium to a taste.

The same job becomes a different job depending on how a worker sees it, and that predicts what they change

How a worker holds a job changes what the job is, and how they see it predicts what they go on to change. Wrzesniewski found twenty-eight cleaners in one hospital, all under a single job description, describing two different jobs: one minimal and unskilled, one that counted itself part of healing. Whether people see work as a job, a career or a calling predicts whether they reshape the paid tasks, the visible tasks and powerful people, or the purpose. Vivekananda makes the same point from the other side. Against it, money worries, the standing of the job and workplace rules decide how much room a person actually has.

People keep going for something outside themselves that waits to be done, and it is never finished

What holds a person up is something outside them that is waiting, and it is a direction rather than an arrival. Frankl argues people endure more when a person needs them or work is left that only they can finish, and he turned back two prisoners who meant to kill themselves this way. He also saw the control case: with no known end date a person stops aiming at the future, and a day in the camp felt longer than a week. Hayes says the same from the clinic, that a value is a direction you never finish reaching. Frankl's evidence comes only from survivors.

Science cannot confirm Buddhism or find its states in the brain, and its scientific reputation was built in the 1800s

A scan cannot certify a tradition or locate the state it names. Thompson traces the belief that Buddhism is uniquely rational to nineteenth-century reformers who took a colonial argument, that having science proved Christian superiority, and turned it around. He also argues that finding mindfulness in a brain region explains nothing, since the concept decides what the scanner counts. The language supports him: sati means holding in mind, the same word as the Sanskrit for memory, and bare attention is Nyanaponika's 1954 gloss of one clause. Only two sources, one of them a contested reading, and the case is historical rather than experimental.

Adults grow by turning what they are into something they can look at, and most stop partway

Kegan's mechanism is a shift from being something to being able to look at it: whatever you are cannot be seen by you, and whatever you can hold and examine no longer runs you. The numbers come from a composite of twelve studies, 282 adults, of whom 59 per cent had not reached self-authorship, and over 70 per cent of his longitudinal subjects were short of it on entering. None of the 282 reached the fifth order at all. The composite is not a probability sample and is whiter, wealthier and better educated than the country, the scoring is interpretive, and a stage with no positive cases says as much about the instrument as about people.

Knowing which group someone belongs to tells you little about how they will act

Group membership predicts conduct poorly, and reading an individual off their category misses the person in front of you. Frankl says knowing whether a man was a guard or a prisoner told you almost nothing, since one camp commander bought medicine with his own money and a senior prisoner was harder than any guard. Epley supplies the mechanism: a mind you cannot read is treated as smaller rather than as unknown, so distant groups are judged less able to feel shame or remorse and their apologies count for less. Only two claims and two sources, and Frankl's half is an observation from a single extreme setting.

Reminding a person of a value outside the threatened area lets them take in bad news about it

Cohen and Sherman's field trials had students spend ten minutes writing about something they personally valued: in three middle schools the share of African American students earning a D or F in the first term halved, and the gain persisted. The values that work reach beyond the self, compassion or service, while power, status and approval do nothing, and affirming inside the threatened area makes people more defensive. James arrives at the same repair from the other end, lowering what you have staked yourself on rather than raising what you achieve. The effect is concentrated in the most threatened students, is absent without a threat and some ability waiting to be used, and a British medical-school study found mixed results.

The brain builds a picture of itself and cannot see that it is a picture, so the self feels real

Metzinger argues the brain builds a picture of itself and hides the building, because hiding it is cheaper than showing it, and whatever falls inside that picture arrives feeling like yours. The rubber-hand illusion moves the boundary in sixty to ninety seconds, and Lenggenhager, Metzinger and Blanke moved where people felt themselves to be a couple of metres across a room by filming a back being stroked and showing it ahead. Thompson stands against the conclusion twice: every illusion is a construction but not every construction is an illusion, and the no-self result holds only if a self must be single and unbuilt.

A description is never the thing it describes, and trouble starts when a person or machine acts on it instead

Christian's closing argument is that the danger is not machines taking over but the formal descriptions we hand them of what exists and what we want, since a system that runs on such a description reshapes the world to fit it — the car that killed Elaine Herzberg had no category for her. Gaudapada makes the same move against a description in words, arguing that every account of one thing causing another contradicts itself. Both are arguments rather than findings. Christian's is broad enough that little could count against it, and Gaudapada's trilemma defeats only a substance account of causation, not the working notion science uses.

A self that is built is still real, and what counts as one depends on your definition and level

Thompson grants that the brain assembles the self and denies that this makes it an illusion, since every illusion is a construction but not every construction is an illusion. The no-self conclusion, he argues, follows only from defining a self as single, separate and not built from experience; define it as built over time and socially, as James did in 1890 and Mead in 1934, and the same evidence proves much less. Sarvapriyananda's lectures add a level-dependent version, with an immune cell, the bee and the hive each a self. Nothing here is measured, and Metzinger's reply stands against it, that the self is a model the brain cannot see as a model.

AI harms the people using it first, by taking their attention and lowering their view of what humans do

The danger argued for here is not a machine waking up but what these machines do to the people using them. Seth holds that mistaking AI for minds lowers what we think humans are, and that machines which merely seem conscious are the closer problem. Metzinger adds that directing your own attention is one of the deepest parts of being a person, so an industry built to capture attention takes away part of selfhood rather than just time. All three claims are opinion from two philosophy sources with nothing measured, and neither author separates this harm from the older complaint about advertising.

After all the teaching the last choice is the person's own, and they can always choose their attitude

Two books end on the same note: after seven hundred verses Krishna tells Arjuna to reflect and then do as he chooses, and Frankl writes that everything can be taken from a person except the choice of what attitude to take. Both then undercut it. Four verses earlier the Gita has Arjuna's own nature compelling him to fight regardless, and two verses later comes an imperative; Frankl concedes that on average only those survived who had lost all scruples, which makes his evidence a sample of the lucky. Nothing is measured on either side, and one example of a man giving away his bread proves a possibility, not a rule.

An editor's choice of how to read a scripture decides what the scripture is taken to claim

Easwaran presents Krishna as the Self within and the battlefield as the mind, and says openly that this is his choice rather than the only reading; chapters 16 and 18, with their duty and social order, resist it. Shankara, a millennium earlier, applies the same kind of rule, reading each line for the job it is doing before what it plainly says, so a verse written to praise a lesser practice cannot be used to abolish a greater one. Both principles are unfalsifiable, since any awkward verse can be reclassified. Traditions that take the war as a war have read the same verses for as long, and Easwaran's only reply is to practise it and see.

Look through your experience for the one who owns it and you find only the experience itself

Search everything you can find in experience for whoever owns it and only the experience turns up. James reports that the inner self he could locate was movements in the head and throat, and he drops the Soul because it explains nothing and guarantees nothing, since the passing thought takes the one before it as its own and hands the title on. The Anattalakkhana Sutta runs the same search with a control test, that anything you cannot command is not your self, across eleven categories chosen so nothing can hide. Two sources, five opinion and two contested claims, nothing measured, and the Buddha never says that no self exists.

Practice does not produce the goal, and a session that feels calm and successful can be a failed one

The Mandukya Karika names four ways meditation fails, and the one that matters is a mind still stained that looks from outside exactly like a mind at rest, which leaves a practitioner with no test. Rahula presses the same point on the deepest absorptions, which the Buddha learned from his teachers, was not satisfied by, and classed as a pleasant abiding: anything produced by a cause is conditioned, so nirvana is not an effect of the path. Gaudapada extends it to his own words, which he calls a device to be thrown away. Nothing here is measured, and the canon also shows the Buddha using the absorptions he is said to have demoted.

Whatever notices a feeling is not itself in it, and you can see this while the feeling lasts

Whatever notices a state is not itself in that state, and the shift can be made while the state is still running. Drig-Drishya Viveka's line is that whatever notices fear is not afraid, its meditations keep pointing back to whoever is having the experience rather than to the experience, and it says enlightenment does not stop pain but changes who is watching it. Hayes reaches the same position from therapy, calling the observing self a viewpoint rather than one of your thoughts. Four opinion claims from two sources, nothing measured, and the evidence for the shift is a report of the kind these texts elsewhere distrust.

You spot someone who has let go by how evenly they treat opposites, not by what they do

The test offered is not what a person does but whether their reaction still swings between opposites. The Gita checks the freed person by evenness across gold and clay and across people liked and disliked, and Chatterjee says the same stance can be trained by regular reflection, the sign of success being that people you like, dislike and feel nothing for are treated alike. Against it stands the Ashtavakra Gita, whose liberated man is described so fully that nothing in the description separates him from someone who is simply idle. Two opinion claims from two sources, one contested claim against, and no feedback that could fail the test.

A habit you keep failing to break is protecting you, and small tests of the fear behind it work

Kegan and Lahey argue that repeated failure to change is not weak willpower but a second commitment the failure serves, so the way out is to find the fear behind it and run small, safe tests of it. Their coaching cases show people with the same goal and behaviour having entirely different hidden commitments, and a humanities department that had tenured nobody in eleven years moved only once someone said aloud what it was protecting. The evidence is selected cases from their own practice with no controls, the opening one-in-seven heart-patients figure carries no citation, and the rule that a first answer is a cover cannot be tested from inside the method.

Fighting a painful feeling costs more than the feeling, and willingness to feel it predicts how well you function

Hayes separates the pain a person feels from the effort spent warding it off, and puts the damage in the second. In chronic pain the measured physical damage barely predicts reported disability, while willingness and the ability to act while hurting do. Wegner's demonstration supports the mechanism: told not to think of a yellow Jeep, people think of it more. The outcome evidence is not in dispute, over a thousand trials in twenty years and NICE guidance since 2021, with Öst's reviews putting the mean effect at 0.68 and later 0.42 and no significant advantage over other therapies. What is contested is the explanation, which rests on a questionnaire that may measure how bad people feel.

Writing about your values helps only when it comes early, nobody explains its purpose, and its gains build on themselves

Cohen and Sherman's review finds three conditions on the ten-minute values-writing exercise. It works before a threat or soon after, but not once the person has already talked themselves round; it loses its force when people are told what it is for, which is why British medical students whose essays instructors read and graded showed no benefit; and a brief effect lasts only where it starts a loop of better performance and better treatment. The loop is an explanation offered after the fact, the timing comparison in schools was between weeks of a term rather than randomised, and a second year of booster sessions added nothing.

How much a person suffers depends on how they see it, not on the size of what happened

Frankl says suffering behaves like a gas, filling whatever space it is given, so a small trouble can take up as much of a person as a great one. His second observation runs the same way: numbness protected prisoners rather than damaging them, and what still reached a man through it was not physical pain but being treated unjustly, the blow in the bread line hurting less than its unreasonableness. Both come from one observer recording his own reactions in the camps, with nothing measured. The comparison also undoes itself, since if size is entirely relative then no suffering can be measured against another, including the comparisons the book invites.

The self is a pattern the brain makes by watching itself, built from parts that contain no self

Hofstadter's account is that a self appears when a system watches itself closely enough to build symbols about itself, and that it cannot see the machinery underneath. He takes Gödel as the formal result: any system able to describe patterns ends up containing statements about itself, even where the designers tried to rule that out. He also argues that a machine with no memory and no imagination has no self, and that a pattern rather than its parts can be the real cause. One source and five claims, four of them opinion, and the Gödel step is an analogy rather than a proof about brains.

What feels warm and yours counts as part of you, so belongings come in and old selves drop out

James puts the edge of a self wherever feeling reaches. A man's clothes and property are counted in, he has one social self for every group whose opinion matters to him, and a past self is his only where warmth and continuity still reach. The evidence is Reverend Ansel Bourne, who drew money in Providence on 17 January 1887 and vanished, then on 14 March woke in Norristown as a shopkeeper of six weeks trading as A. J. Brown and would not believe two months had passed. One source, four claims, three of them opinion, and a single dissociation case carries the weight.

A person and the tool they rely on solve the task together, and where the work happens decides nothing

Clark and Chalmers argue that if a process would count as thinking when it happens in the head, it counts when part of it happens outside — Otto, who has amnesia, believes what his notebook says before he opens it, the way you believe what you are about to recall. The case is built on the two-way traffic between person and resource, in Tetris and in the notebook, and nothing in the paper is measured. Two claims stand against it: Adams and Aizawa reply that the notebook is coupled to memory rather than part of it, and a store you did not fill and cannot vouch for fails the authors' own conditions.

A person rejects a true account of themselves when the belief protects them, so argument alone does not move it

Rahula traces the idea of a self to two needs: people made God out of a need for protection and an immortal soul out of a need to go on existing, so a teaching that removes both meets resistance that has nothing to do with the evidence. One source carries the whole claim and nothing is measured. The argument cuts against itself, since explaining why a belief is held says nothing about whether it is true, and the same story would explain the belief if there were a self. Kegan and Lahey show that a protective commitment can be mapped and revised by the person holding it, where an account pitched at the whole species leaves nobody anything to do.

An outside store counts as part of your mind only under conditions most stores fail to meet

Clark and Chalmers list four conditions for counting an outside store as memory: it is there when needed, easy to get at, taken as true when retrieved, and put there by you in the first place. Otto's notebook holds what Otto wrote; the Internet, and anything else you did not fill and have never endorsed, fails the test. The list is the authors' own, offered as a way of sorting cases rather than as a criterion, with no weighting and no scale, and they weaken the fourth condition themselves. Whether the endorsement conditions are needed at all is still disputed, and one paper carries the whole case.

How much of a mind something has is a matter of degree, and how much it is owed follows

Hofstadter argues that having a soul is a question of how much rather than whether, with beings sitting at different points on one scale, and he accepts the consequence that they differ in how much consideration they are owed. The unit of measurement is his own invention and he says so; there is no procedure for placing anything on the scale, so it cannot be shown wrong about any case. One source carries the whole claim, marked contested, with nothing recorded against it. Over's 2021 argument cuts against the use it is usually put to, that people who treat others cruelly understand perfectly well how human their victims are.

Judgment fails at the end of a chain that begins with what you dwell on, not at the decision

Gita 2.62 and 2.63 set out a sequence with seven steps: dwelling on something leads to attachment, then desire, then anger, then delusion, then confused memory, and only at the end the loss of judgment. The practical point is that the place to intervene is the first step, not the last. One verse pair from one source carries it, and nothing is measured. These are states a person can notice in themselves, offered as a causal chain, with no evidence that the links run in that order or that breaking an early one prevents the later ones.

The person inside a situation sees it least clearly, including when they write about it later

Being inside a situation is the worst position from which to describe it, and writing the account afterwards does not fix that. The one supporting claim is Frankl's own admission that on average only those survived who had lost all scruples, which makes him one of the lucky ones reporting from inside his own sample. It governs how every other Frankl claim should be read. The support is a single contested claim from a single source, it is an argument about sampling rather than a finding, and nothing here shows an outside observer would have done better.

You have a claim on your work and none on its results, and what you drop is the claim

Gita 2.47 gives a person a right to the action and never to what it produces, and 2.48 defines the discipline as staying even in success and failure. Easwaran reads what is given up as selfish wanting rather than work or possessions, so charity can fail the test and cooking a meal can pass; the verse's fourth clause closes the exit by forbidding attachment to doing nothing. All five claims are the text's instruction, with nothing offered as evidence and no test an outsider could run, since the test sits in a state of mind. Chapter 12 also puts giving up results last on its ladder and then calls it the highest.
